mappingNote: Booklet filename levels follow booklets.ts BAND_TO_LEVEL, verified at ingest. Age ranges are copied from bands.ts: little (5–10) = elementary; young (11–14) = middle; emerging (15–18) = high; adult (Adult) = adult. Books whose titles name an age use that band. Other books (parent manuals, full readers, operator books) are tagged adult; age-leveled booklets carry the child bands.

bands.name: Little Thinkers
bands.promise: Stories, one idea, one small act. AI is a tool in the room — never a secret friend.
bands.sitting: 15–20 minutes. A grown-up in the room.
bands.aiRule: Conversation only. Hint, then stop. No homework answers. No names, photos, or school. If it feels confusing or unkind, ask a grown-up.
bands.hermes: One step. A short story. Ask a Grown-Up. Conversation only. Do not clone an adult profile.

bands.name: Young Minds
bands.promise: Scenarios, projects, and honest talk. Learn to catch a confident wrong answer — including your own.
bands.aiRule: Hint, then example. Never a ghostwriter. Optional local voice or image understanding if a parent turns it on. Talk About It before you paste anything.
bands.hermes: Hint, then example. Talk About It. Chat. Optional local voice-to-text. Optional image understanding.

bands.name: Emerging Adults
bands.promise: Real argument. Agent design. Integrity you can defend. Philosophy as preparation for a world that will not grade your character.
bands.aiRule: You write. The guide critiques. Optional narrow search or school files a parent approves. Not an adult team agent. Cite what you used.
bands.hermes: Real argument. Practice. Reflect. Chat. Optional narrow search or school files. Not an adult team agent.

bands.name: Lifelong Learners
bands.promise: Full depth. The operating model: inspect, test, refuse. Teach without handing a child your own agent.
bands.aiRule: You are the operator. Give the child a new, simpler profile for their age — or no profile. Do not copy yours. Official Hermes docs win if a command is out of date.
bands.hermes: The adult profile is yours. Child profiles are separate. Design, approve, test with fake examples, then invite the child.

subjects.name: Autonomous AI
subjects.promise: What an agent is, what it is not, and how to stay the operator.
subjects.aiSpine: Every sitting practices the rule: try first, hint second, evaluate always, parent in the loop.

subjects.name: Critical Thinking
subjects.promise: Claims, counterclaims, and what would change your mind.
subjects.aiSpine: Treat every model output as a classmate's draft: interesting, unchecked, not a source.

subjects.name: Wisdom & Philosophy
subjects.promise: The Stoics and the examined life, rewritten for the age in the chair.
subjects.aiSpine: The booklet is the text. The guide asks; it does not recite. Inner freedom is not an app setting.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.promise: Estimate, show the method, then ask a tool to check the path — never the soul of the work.
subjects.aiSpine: AI may review a method you already wrote. It may not be the first hand that touches the problem.

subjects.name: Science
subjects.promise: Hypothesis before search. The universe is not a chatbot.
subjects.aiSpine: Write the guess and the test. Then, if you ask a model, hunt for what would prove it wrong.

subjects.name: English
subjects.promise: You write the draft. The guide is an editor who asks questions, not an author with your name on it.
subjects.aiSpine: No hidden AI homework. If a sentence isn't yours, it doesn't go in the folder.

subjects.name: History
subjects.promise: Primary sources first. Summaries — human or machine — are claims.
subjects.aiSpine: A model that compresses the past will flatten the people in it. Check the source.

subjects.name: Art
subjects.promise: Hands before generate. Taste is a muscle. Tools are not a substitute for seeing.
subjects.aiSpine: Make something ugly on purpose. Then discuss what a generator averages away.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.promise: Specify the agent: soul, tools, refuse-list. Code is permission made explicit.
subjects.aiSpine: Autonomy is a design choice. If a tool is on, you chose it. If it is off, that is the lesson.

subjects.name: World Languages
subjects.promise: Say it yourself. A model can drill; it cannot take the exam of being understood.
subjects.aiSpine: Practice partner, not ghost-speaker. Record your own mouth. The guide waits.

paths.name: Education in the Age of AI
paths.promise: The spine: autonomous use, integrity, and a mind that can refuse a fluent wrong answer.

paths.name: Character
paths.promise: Agency, anger, time, and duty — the Stoic year, practiced in the room.

paths.name: Letters & Worlds
paths.promise: Write, read sources, speak. The human work that models compress.

paths.name: Number & Nature
paths.promise: Estimate, hypothesize, measure. Tools after the mind has moved.

paths.name: Maker
paths.promise: Hands, systems, and taste. Generate last.

units.subject: ai
units.title: Education in the Age of AI
units.blurb: Tool vs person, try first, fluent error, permissions, privacy, a full sitting with a guide.

units.subject: ai
units.title: Building a Week with an Agent
units.blurb: Eval harnesses, memory hygiene, permissions audit, and when to turn the agent off.

units.subject: thinking
units.title: How to Think
units.blurb: Claim and check, steel-man, what would change your mind, say what you mean, catch a fluent claim, then the full loop.

units.subject: thinking
units.title: Bias, Frames, and Missing Voices
units.blurb: Whose data trained the room you are standing in.

units.subject: philosophy
units.title: Character — The Stoics
units.blurb: Epictetus, Marcus, Seneca — same arc, four depths. Circle, citadel, time.

units.subject: philosophy
units.title: Zeno — The Founder
units.blurb: Virtue as the only good. Shipwreck as curriculum. Seeds of reason, the world city, living according to nature, and the founder's legacy.

units.subject: philosophy
units.title: How the Greeks Thought
units.blurb: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Pre-Socratics — question, form, cause. From method to metaphysics.

units.subject: philosophy
units.title: Faith & Reason
units.blurb: Church Fathers through Aquinas. Belief that can think. Parent theological humility notes.

units.subject: philosophy
units.title: The Intellectual History of AI
units.blurb: Turing's question, Searle's Chinese Room, Wiener's genie. The three ideas every AI user should know.

units.subject: math
units.title: Estimate Before the Oracle
units.blurb: A number in the head before a tool in the hand. Little arc: guess, path, catch a wild number, two ways, about, then the machine.

units.subject: math
units.title: Show the Path
units.blurb: Proof as a sentence other people can walk.

units.subject: science
units.title: Hypothesis Before Search
units.blurb: The universe is not a chatbot. Write the guess first.

units.subject: science
units.title: Measure Twice
units.blurb: Error, units, and the temptation to ask a model instead of a scale.

units.subject: english
units.title: You Write It
units.blurb: Draft by hand. The guide is an editor who asks, not an author who signs your name.

units.subject: english
units.title: Rhetoric in the Age of Fluency
units.blurb: Ethos, pathos, logos — and the machine that fakes all three.

units.subject: history
units.title: Source Before Summary
units.blurb: A paragraph from then, before anyone — human or model — compresses it.

units.subject: history
units.title: Citizens — Constitution & Declaration
units.blurb: Primary text, not storybook propaganda. A republic is a moral practice.

units.subject: history
units.title: Magna Carta — The Charter and the Chain
units.blurb: A feudal contract that became the rule of law. The chain from Runnymede to your rights.

units.subject: history
units.title: The Constitution — Designed, Not Extracted
units.blurb: Power against power, the losers' legacy, the three-fifths sin, and the amendment chain. How the Constitution grows.

units.subject: history
units.title: The Declaration — The Promise and the Gap
units.blurb: Self-evident truths, the right of revolution, and the gap between the promise and the practice. The chain from 1776 to today.

units.subject: history
units.title: The Federalist — The Brief That Sold the Machine
units.blurb: A New York sales campaign, not the Constitution. Faction vs Brutus, ambition, judgment without sword, the lost argument for a bill of rights, and the civic chain.

units.subject: history
units.title: The Fourteenth Amendment — The Answer After the War
units.blurb: The Constitution answering Fed 54 and Dred Scott. Section 1 in four clauses. Gettysburg as speech, not instrument. Ugly clauses named. Writing is not keeping.

units.subject: history
units.title: Look First — History for Little Thinkers
units.blurb: Look at a real thing first. Who held it. Then not now. Two tellers. Keep the piece. Tell it back.

units.subject: english
units.title: Stories and Voices — Letters for Little Thinkers
units.blurb: Tell it in your own words. The story behind a real thing. Hear it and say it back.

units.subject: art
units.title: Hand Before Generate
units.blurb: Make something imperfect. Then look at what a generator averages away.

units.subject: art
units.title: Taste Is a Muscle
units.blurb: Looking longer than the feed. Copy from life, not from a prompt.

units.subject: cs
units.title: Specify the Agent
units.blurb: Soul, tools, refuse-list. Autonomy is a design choice. Paper first. Do not build tonight.

units.subject: cs
units.title: Eval or It Did Not Happen
units.blurb: Synthetic tests, CI gates, eval-driven development, and the full eval cycle. The kit's EVALS.md is the model.

units.subject: language
units.title: Say It Yourself
units.blurb: The mouth has to move. Hear, say, use, ask, catch the ghost-speaker. A model can drill; it cannot be understood for you.

units.subject: language
units.title: A Second Tongue, a Second Mind
units.blurb: Conversation ladders, not subtitle crutches.

items.text: 1 Art for Emerging Adults Michael Gannotti A homeschool teaching manual for ages 15–18. Illustrated teaching-manual edition, 28 September 2026. Notes run in one series at the back. Chapter-opening images are original still-lifes, not portraits of people. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to use this book • If you only remember five things • The Art Hour • Chapter 1 — What art looks like at 15–18 • Chapter 2 — The sketchbook, the studio, and adult tools • Chapter 3 — Drawing from life: figure, portrait, and place • Chapter 4 — Painting: watercolor, gouache, and acrylic • Chapter 5 — Photography, digital art, and design • Chapter 6 — Art history and contemporary art • Chapter 7 — Critique and the artist statement • Chapter 8 — Portfolio, assessment, and progress checks • Chapter 9 — Records, credit, and next steps • Chapter 10 — Resources • A Note on Sources • Notes 3 Welcome You do not need to be an artist to mentor a fifteen- to eighteen-year-old through a real year of art. You need to protect the time, set up a safe corner, ask good questions, find outside eyes, and keep honest records. Your student does the looking and the making, and more and more, the leading. That is what this book is for. A Thursday, for example It is a little after two in the afternoon. A small mirror is clamped to the edge of a table by the window, and a desk lamp is angled so that one side of the mirror’s reflection is in light and the other in shadow. A sixteen-year-old has been working on a self-portrait for forty minutes. The board is propped against the table edge. A pencil is held out at arm’s length, one eye closed, measuring. Her mother comes in with a mug of tea, sets it on the shelf by the door (nothing to eat or drink at the art table; that rule has been in the house for a year now), and asks one question: “Where are you looking hardest?” The student doesn’t look up. “The shadow under my cheekbone. I thought it was one shape. It’s three.” Her mother nods, says, “Good. I’ll leave you to it,” and leaves. That is most of the job. An hour later there is a dated drawing, a phone photo of it in the family archive, a line in the hour log (Thurs, 55 min, self-portrait session 2), and a note in the sketchbook margin: three shadow shapes — the middle one is the lightest. Nobody said the drawing was good or bad. The student will decide that for herself, later, with reasons. (That Thursday is a composite, drawn from common situations. It is not a real family. You will meet a few more like it in this book, and each one is labelled.) The student you actually have Fifteen to eighteen is a remarkable age for art, and a demanding one. Your student can do real work. Many can render some things convincingly and hold a piece across several sessions. They can use adult materials under clear rules. They can run a critique, write 4 WELCOME 5 about their own work, and plan a week. They are also hard on themselves. A student who can draw a convincing eye can see exactly what is wrong with the other one. Their taste often runs ahead of their hand: they love work they cannot yet make, and the gap can feel like a verdict. They want a voice of their own, sometimes before they have had the chance to find out what they care about. Their time is pulled in many directions: a job, driving lessons, heavier academic courses, friends. And their work has audiences everywhere: friends, social feeds, contest judges, admissions readers, AP scorers. Each wants something slightly different. None of this is a problem to fix. The self-criticism means they can see. The taste means they know where they want to go. The wish for a voice is the start of a real body of work, if it can be turned into a question and pursued across many pieces instead of a style chosen on the first day. At this age the question is less can you draw? and more what will you choose to look at, and will you stay with it? This book is built around that question. Why this matters now In the 2016 national survey of homeschooling families, art was being taught to 78 percent of homeschooled students in the earliest grades and to fewer than a third (29 percent) of homeschooled high schoolers.1 The survey does not say why. It does suggest that high school is where art most often slips off the week. It is also the age when art can count most. A year of honest studio work can become a high-school credit with a plain title, a portfolio for college or art school if your student wants one, and, more lasting than either, a habit of looking and making that goes with them into adult life. What a good week looks like A good week of art at this age is not heroic. On Monday your student writes a short plan and you initial it. Two or three times that week they chair an Art Hour of about an hour: a few minutes of silent looking, ten minutes of thumbnails, a long stretch of making, a short critique they run, and a few minutes of filing. Every day, Hour or not, there is a dated sketchbook page of ten to fifteen minutes. Somewhere in the week there is studio time they chose for themselves. Every week or two there is an outing: a museum with one question, a gallery, a park bench, a community class. On Friday there is a five-minute File: what happened, the hours, one next step. That is it. Some weeks will be thinner, because of exams, a job, a family week away. A thin week with a daily page in it still counts. The habit is the thing, and the habit is small enough to survive a busy house. What you actually do Your jobs are ones you can do well starting this week: WELCOME 6 • Protect the time. Two or three Art Hours a week, a short daily sketchbook page, and some open studio time. • Set up the studio safely. A corner with light, moving air, and a place for everything. The rules are in The Art Hour, stated once. • Ask good questions. Each chapter gives you the exact words. Then you wait. • Find outside eyes. A community class, a co-op critique, a portfolio review, a working artist who will talk for half an hour. When your student outgrows what you can show them, that is good news. • Keep honest records. Hours, dates, photos of finished work, a course title a stranger can read. None of these jobs needs you to draw well. All of them need you to show up, and the student notices when you do. You may also learn alongside. A parent who keeps a cheap sketchbook of their own, and doesn’t show it off, teaches more about practice than any speech. The focus of the whole book See long before you judge; sketch before you polish; sign only what you made. See long before you judge means staying with a hard drawing, a strange contemporary painting, or your own portfolio long enough to find evidence before deciding anything. Sketch before you polish means thumbnails, studies, and honest ugly middles come before the resolved piece. They are the work, not the warm-up. Sign only what you made means authorship. Your student discloses tools, references, and help; credits every source; and puts their name only on marks and choices that are theirs. If you used Art for Young Minds with this student a few years ago, you will recognize the first two clauses. The third arrives now because at fifteen to eighteen the work starts going out into the world with a name on it. Two readers at once Most of this book talks to you, the parent, as co-teacher and mentor. Each teaching chapter also has a section headed For the student, written directly to your fifteen- to eighteen-year-old. Hand it over. It is short, it is written for someone nearly grown, and it is meant to be used without you in the room. What this book will not do It will not hand you a 180-day plan. You get a week the student plans, a pacing sketch for the year, and the judgment to choose. WELCOME 7 It will not sell you a curriculum or rank programs. The resources chapter describes options by fit and starts with what is free. It will not promise admission to any school, an AP score, a scholarship, or a prize. It will not tell you art makes students smarter at reading or math. The large reviews of that question found no good evidence that it does.2,3 Art is worth teaching for what art teaches: close looking, sustained work on hard problems, decisions you can explain, and the ability to talk honestly about a made thing. It is not a rehash of the earlier books. Art for Little Thinkers (ages 5–10) and Art for Young Minds (ages 11–14) come before this one on the WisdomForge Art Hour ladder; Art for Homeschooling gives a grades 1–12 overview. This book teaches fifteen to eighteen, in depth. It will never treat a generated image as your student’s work, or a model-written statement as their words. It uses no nude figure references. People in this book are drawn clothed, with their consent. It will not put a brand on the transcript. There is no course called “Emerging Adults Art I.” Chapter 9 gives you titles a stranger can read. Encouragement that is specific This week, you can learn to ask one question, “Where are you looking hardest?”, and leave the room. Today, your student can date a sketchbook page and draw one thing in front of them for fifteen minutes. That is enough to begin. — Michael Gannotti How to use this book Read The Art Hour together. It takes about half an hour, and it holds the session shape, the week the student plans, the talk-box shape, the safety spine, and the AI rules that every later chapter points back to. Then you read the parent sections of Chapter 1, and your student reads Chapter 1’s section For the student. Then start. That is the whole on-ramp. You do not need to read the book cover to cover, and you do not need to shop first. A sketchbook, a few pencils, a pen, a lamp, and whatever is on the kitchen table will carry the first two weeks. This week’s shape 1. Monday: the student writes the plan. One line per session on a card or the inside cover of the sketchbook. You read it and initial it. In the first month at 15–16, you write it together. 2. Two or three Art Hours, about 45–60 minutes each, chaired by your student using the five beats in The Art Hour. 3. The daily page, 10–15 minutes, every day, Hour or not. 4. Studio time as your student chooses, on the current piece. 5. One out-of-home try-it every week or two: a museum with a question, a gallery, a park, a community class. 6. Friday File: what happened, the hours, one next step. Five minutes. You initial it. Here is one real-looking week. Treat it as a sample, not an assignment. Day What happens Monday Student writes the plan; Art Hour: daily page started, blind contour of the hand, baseline check Daily page Art Hour: a student-chaired look at one real painting; nine thumbnails for a still life Daily page; 40 minutes of studio time on the still life Art Hour: the still life continued; Friday File and hour log Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday 8 HOW TO USE THIS BOOK 9 Day What happens Saturday Museum or gallery visit with one question, if the week allows Daily page Sunday Most chapters take three to six weeks. Some take longer, and that is fine. Placement: skill and independence, not birthday Inside every teaching chapter you will see two planning bands: 15–16 and 17–18. The 15–16 moves assume you are in the room when a new tool or material appears, a range of media rather than depth in one, student-led critique with a simple question card, and short written statements. The 17–18 moves assume longer independent studio blocks, a sustained investigation (one question pursued across many works), a more formal critique the student chairs, writing to real limits, outside venues you have checked, and, if your family chooses, solvent-free oil painting. Use the bands as a guide, not a lock. A fifteen-year-old with four years of serious drawing behind them may work in the 17–18 moves. An eighteen-year-old starting art in senior year begins with the 15–16 moves, and there is nothing lost by it. Nobody in this book is “behind.” A “grade 11 art” book is a publisher’s scope, not a legal level. Ho…

Documents still constrain the facts. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The Studio Hour • Chapter 1 — Grades 1–2: Material play: the hand in the stuff • Chapter 2 — Grades 3–5: Observation starts: what you actually see • Chapter 3 — Grades 6–8: Proportion, space, and a page that takes more than one sitting • Chapter 4 — Drawing • Chapter 5 — Painting • Chapter 6 — Sculpture • Chapter 7 — Design and Color • Chapter 8 — Looking and the Portfolio • Chapter 9 — Records • Chapter 10 — Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome This book exists because the studio hour at your table is the whole program. There is no art room down the hall and no specialist waiting after lunch. There is you, a student, paper, and today’s idea — a line to try, a mug to look at, a lump of clay to pinch. That is enough, if you know what to do with the hour. I wrote this for a capable, busy, willing parent. You may be teaching two ages at once. You may be fitting art between a job, a toddler, and a grocery run. You may have loved making things, or you may remember drawing as something other people did well. Many adults feel rusty when they sit down to draw. That feeling is common. It is not a verdict. We will move on from it. This book will make you fluent enough in today’s idea to notice a stuck hand and ask a good question — without taking over the brush. You do not need to be a studio artist. You do need to understand this week’s idea well enough to see that a child is drawing the name of a mug instead of this mug from here. You need a session shape you can run on a Tuesday. You need a few sentences that actually help. That is the job. A path through making — from first-grade material play through a high-school sequence a stranger can read — is possible at a kitchen table. The path is not a personality trait, a gifted label, or a fridge picture. It is a sequence of ideas, practiced until they hold, with you in the chair. About 3.4 percent of U.S. students ages 5–17 were homeschooled in 2022–23 — roughly 1.765 million children.1 That figure is context, not a ranking. You are 1 Ellena Sempeles and Jiashan Cui, Parent and Family Involvement in Education: 2023, NCES 2024-113 (Washington, DC: National Center for Education Statistics, September 2024), Table A-6: 3.4 percent homeschooled, approximately 1,765,000 students, ages 5–17 with a K–12 grade equivalent, 2022–23. https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2024/2024113.pdf. Access date for URLs in these notes: 31 August 2026. Latest federal count this book uses; not a 2026 national total. A neighboring 5.2 4 WELCOME 5 one of those tables. Homeschooling is legal in all fifty states and the District of Columbia. The paperwork is not one load: Texas asks almost nothing of the state agency; New York asks for a written plan and regular reports.2 There is no national homeschool diploma and no national art credit a registrar already files.3 In the last federal subject tables, art was taught that year to 53 percent of K–12-equivalent homeschoolers — common in the early grades, less so later. Among ninth- through twelfth-grade homeschoolers, 29 percent were being taught art that year.4 That is a picture of practice, not a scold. A family that takes Drawing, Painting, or Sculpture as a real high-school sequence is walking a path, not copying a typical year. The hour in front of you is the work. percent received instruction at home (homeschooled or full-time virtual) and is a different bucket. 2 Texas Education Agency, “Home Schooling,” https://tea.texas.gov/families-andstudents/finding-school-your-child/home-schooling. New York State Education Department, “Home Instruction Questions and Answers,” https://www.nysed.gov/nonpublic-schools/homeinstruction-questions-and-answers. Homeschooling is legal in all fifty states and D.C.; these two pages illustrate a light-process and a heavier-process pattern, not a national template. This book is not legal advice. 3 Texas Education Agency, “Home Schooling”: “The State of Texas does not award a diploma to students that are home schooled.” New York State Education Department, “Home Instruction Questions and Answers”: a high school diploma “may only be awarded to a student enrolled in a registered secondary school.” NCAA Eligibility Center, Home School Toolkit 2025–26, http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/eligibility_center/Student_Resources/Home_School_Toolkit.pdf, treats proof of graduation as a family- or umbrella-issued artifact. Art is not an NCAA core course. 4 Jiashan Cui and Rachel Hanson, Homeschooling in the United States: Results from the 2012 and 2016 Parent and Family Involvement in Education Surveys, NCES 2020-001 (Washington, DC: National Center for Education Statistics, December 2019), Table 9: among K–12-equivalent homeschoolers, art taught that year 53 percent overall (78 percent K–2, 63 percent 3–5, 50 percent 6–8, 29 percent 9–12). https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2020/2020001.pdf. The 2023 First Look did not republish subject-taught tables. WELCOME 6 Figure 2: A kitchen-table studio setup What a good studio hour looks like You sit down already knowing today’s idea. The child warms up by looking: what is actually there on the table, not what they remember a mug looks like. You demo one move, short — a contour, a pinch, a wash. Then they try, and you wait. You ask one looking question — not “is it pretty?” but “What do you see?” Practice mixes the new move with last week’s. The hour ends with one short piece they do alone: a drawing, a pinch, a page they can talk about. You stop talking sooner than feels polite. The child holds the tool. You hold the key — the setup, the time, the question. That is the hour. The next long piece of this front matter, The Studio Hour, will teach it in full. Later chapters will not reinvent it. The hour is justified by looking and making. Visual art is not a reliable way to raise reading or math scores, and this book will not sell it as one.5 You put paper on the 5 Ellen Winner and Lois Hetland, Reviewing Education and the Arts Project executive summary, Journal of Aesthetic Education 34, nos. 3–4 (Fall/Winter 2000); reprinted in NAEA Translations, WELCOME 7 table because the child needs to see, to choose a mark, to think through a material, and to have a folder a stranger can open. Those are the moves. The chapters will give you wording. The hour will stay this shape. What you will actually get Each teaching chapter does eight jobs, always in the same order, so you are never hunting for the move. You will learn why this week’s idea is worth the struggle — what it unlocks later. You will understand the idea yourself, in plain language, with one everyday picture and one precise picture, and with the stuck hands you should be able to notice. You will get a session you can run this week, including exact wording and named projects: materials, time, mess, the fun of it, the skill it builds. You will get practice that builds looking and making, not a pile of identical crafts. Your student will get a short section of their own. If it isn’t clicking, you will get three diagnostics and a next move for each, with no shame in the room. Tools, including AI, stay optional and adult-side. And you will get a plain checklist for “done enough,” so you can place by skill rather than by birthday. The eight teaching chapters follow the work, not twelve thin grade labels: material play in grades 1–2; observation drawing, watercolor, and a first sketchbook in grades 3–5; proportion, space, and longer projects in grades 6–8; then highschool Drawing (or Art I), Painting, Sculpture, design and color, and looking plus a portfolio a stranger can open. Records and resources come last. This week you can learn the session shape and today’s idea well enough to notice a stuck hand. Today the child can look at one object and make one unaided mark. What this book will not do This book will not hand you 180 days of crafts. A year of photocopied projects is not a teaching method, and I will not pretend it is. Winter 2001: 188 reports; no reliable causal link from arts-rich education to verbal and mathematics scores or grades; visual arts and reading a very small relationship that could not be generalized, and in reading readiness, not reading achievement. “Arts educators should never allow the arts to be justified wholly or even primarily in terms of what the arts can do for mathematics or reading.” WELCOME 8 It will not sell you a curriculum. Later, a short resources chapter names common programs by fit — parent load, process versus copy, religious versus secular, how they place a student, how they shape a high-school credit — so you can choose. Artistic Pursuits, How Great Thou Art, Atelier (the Arts Attack video program, which is not a classical sight-size atelier), Draw Write Now, Usborne how-to books, and a Davis Discovering Drawing path are tools. None of them is this book, and this book is not a catalog in disguise. A family may combine. Combining does not turn a brand into a course name. The transcript still says Drawing, or Art I, or Painting. It will not promise talent, and it will not promise an AP score. There is no guaranteed “gifted” label, no guaranteed fridge picture that looks adult, and no guaranteed AP Art and Design number inside these pages. AP 2-D, AP 3-D, and AP Drawing are optional objects, named later, not this book. What this book can promise is a path: the ideas in order, at the skill the child actually has, until they can do the next idea unaided. National Core Arts Standards are a map you can steal clusters from. They are voluntary. They “have never been a monolithic and prescriptive set of governing rules for curriculum or teaching methods.”6 They are not a homeschool mandate and they are not a method. A publisher’s “grade 6” book is a scope, not a legal grade. Drawing is a body of skill, not a fourteenth-birthday present. Arts for all students, not only for those already labeled talented: that is the map’s own stance, and it matches the promise here.7 It is not an art-history survey. Looking at a work is a studio habit inside the hour — five minutes with one picture, a real question — not a 250-work course. AP Art History is a separate optional object. It does not live in the looking chapter as a dump. And this is not a sequel. Autonomous AI and Education is another book. AI is a lane here: one studio-hour box in this front matter, then a short tools box in each teaching chapter. Image generators do not get the child’s project. Evaluation of a 6 National Coalition for Core Arts Standards, National Core Arts Standards: A Conceptual Framework for Arts Learning (2014), https://nationalartsstandards.org/sites/default/files/NCCAS%20%20Conceptual%20Framework.pdf: “Standards in the United States have never been a monolithic and prescriptive set of governing rules for curriculum or teaching methods.” Released 4 June 2014; voluntary unless a state adopts or adapts them through a formal regulatory process. 7 National Coalition for Core Arts Standards, A Conceptual Framework for Arts Learning, foreword: arts for all students, “not just those identified as ‘talented.’ ” The promise of this book is a path through making, not a talent label. WELCOME 9 mark lives in the looking, not in a course titled AI Art. This is not a book that lectures your child about you, or you about your character. The student is a person, not a percentile and not a talent score. When this book speaks to them, it speaks with respect. No baby-talk. No research sermon. The promise If you only remember one sentence, remember this: a path through making, not a talent myth. The work is to take this child through art — material play,…

items.text: Art for Little Thinkers Michael Gannotti 1 Figure 1: Cover Art for Little Thinkers Michael Gannotti This illustrated edition is the teaching-manual of 24 September 2026. Endnotes run in one series. Chapter-opening images are original still-lifes, not portraits of persons or children. Documents still constrain the facts. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The Art Hour • Chapter 1 — What art looks like at 5–10 • Chapter 2 — Looking at art and objects • Chapter 3 — Mark-making and line • Chapter 4 — Color and paint light • Chapter 5 — Collage, print, and paper • Chapter 6 — Clay and 3-D soft • Chapter 7 — Talking and writing about art • Chapter 8 — Short assessments and progress checks • Chapter 9 — Records • Chapter 10 — Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome You do not need to be a studio artist to teach a five- to ten-year-old real art looking and making. You need an object on the table before the name, and a child’s mark on the child’s page before polish. That is what this book is for. Why this book exists Many adults remember art as coloring sheets, a laminated color wheel, and a quiet “make it nice” from the adult at the elbow. That memory can leave you feeling rusty when a child asks how to draw a dog, or freezes at a blank page, or wants you to finish the ear. Feeling rusty is normal. It is not a character flaw. At ages 5–10, art does not begin with a medium survey or a gallery critique. It begins with looking and making. A child can notice yellow dots on a postcard before anyone says pointillism. A child can follow a mug’s rim with a fat crayon. A child can tear paper and glue a scrap story. A child can pinch soft clay and redesign when a wall falls. A child can say what they see — and what makes them say that — without racing to “pretty.” Those moves are not a waiting room for middle school. They are the work. This book teaches you how to run a short Art Hour at home — roughly twenty to forty minutes — with the object down before the vocabulary, and with look before name and make before polish as the spine. Inside the chapters you will see two planning bands: 5–7 and 8–10. Place your child by skill, not by birthday. 4 WELCOME 5 A careful six-year-old and a fluent nine-year-old may sit in the same looking move on different days. The focus lock for the whole book is simple: Look before name. Make before polish. Hold that, and the rest of the manual becomes practice. What a good Art Hour looks like Picture a kitchen table. Not a museum field trip every day. Not a silent “color this packet” hour. Not a product chase for the fridge. You put a mug, a leaf, fat crayons, or two tempera puddles on the table. You cover any caption that already names the famous work. You ask what the child notices — before you tell them what this is called. You wait. They look. They make one short thing with the tool in their hand. You ask one authentic question about what they see or what the hand tried, and you wait again. Then you name the idea only as far as the looking and the mark can carry. Then you stop talking. You leave one crumb: a sticky notice, a three-word caption, a “whose mark” check, or the child’s choice of what goes on the wall. That is the hour. Library picture-book sits, museum one-work visits, grocery color carts, and nature texture walks motivate. They do not replace the look-beforename move on the table. You will meet the full session shape in The Art Hour. Later chapters point back to it. You do not rebuild the spine every week. Two readers at once This is a teaching manual for the parent or co-teacher at the table, with short student sections a child can actually use. When you read a parent section, you are learning today’s looking-and-making move well enough to hear a wrong turn — a name-first rush, an adult-filled mark, a “draw it nice” freeze, a coloring-book-as-only-hour week, a generated image filed as the child’s work, a demo with no child’s page, a coverage lecture with no object WELCOME 6 on the table. You learn what to say next without grabbing the brush or filling the silence with “pretty.” When your child reads (or hears) a student section, they get respect. No baby-talk. No lecture about you. They get a tiny worked example, two tries, and a chance to explain it back. At 5–7 they can notice before a name, mark freely with fat tools, tear and glue, pinch soft clay, choose whether a page goes on the wall, and say what they see. At 8–10 they can follow a mug’s rim more slowly, try blind contour soft, mix with fewer colors, write a short because-I-see caption, redesign a fallen pinch, and say whose mark is on the page. Write — and speak — as if they can. What this book will not do It will not hand you a 180-day craft dump. It will not sell you a curriculum, crown one program, or promise a score. It will not reprint Art for Homeschooling — that book serves grades 1–12, with later medium courses, portfolio edges, AP Art and Design, and solvent/oil/kiln safety for older work. For that map, see that book once. This book teaches the 5–10 Art Hour. It is not a sequel to History for Little Thinkers, Science for Little Thinkers, Critical Thinking Skills for Little Thinkers, English for Little Thinkers, or Math for Little Thinkers. One pointer each is enough. Then we teach art as looking and making. The grain of those manuals — short hour, talk box, named try-its, exit crumb — rhymes. The content does not mash. Fair-test is science. Piece-from-then is history. Contour and tempera puddles are art. It will not title your subject Little Thinkers Art I. A stranger-readable title is Art. Drawing only when the year’s work is mostly drawing. It will not turn the hour into a culture-war pamphlet. Safe art objects only: a mug, a shoe, a leaf, a pear, a window view, fat crayons, tempera puddles, torn paper, a foam stamp, air-dry clay, a dated sketchbook. No child portraits in generators or book illustrations. No deepfake “artist friend.” It will not pitch “art makes you smarter at reading or math.” Justify art by what art teaches — looking, marking, talking about the work. WELCOME 7 It will not put solvents or craft knives on the kitchen table for this age band. Adult present. Materials with an ACMI AP seal and/or labelled Conforms to ASTM D-4236. Washable tempera and soft clay are enough. It will not ask you to wait until middle school to begin. Children this age can look and make. They do not become artists because someone bought a sample craft kit. How the book is built Front matter tells you how to use the week, five things to remember, and the Art Hour once — including the safety spine and the AI box for ages 5–10, said carefully and only once. Eight teaching chapters follow: what art looks like at 5–10; looking at art and objects; mark-making and line; color and paint light; collage, print, and paper; clay and 3-D soft; talking and writing about art; short assessments and progress checks. Then records and resources. Records keep a dated sketchbook, a looking note, the child’s make, and an optional process photo under Art. Resources name common programs by fit — parent load, look-then-make vs step-by-step, placement — with library, museum, and gallery first. Fit, not rank. Every teaching chapter uses the same eight headings, a talk box with an exact opening question, named try-its inside the home and outside it, and age-band moves for 5–7 and 8–10. Encouragement that is specific This week you can learn one looking move well enough to hear a name-first rush and turn it back to the mug, the leaf, or the page. Today your child can point at one thing they notice and keep their own mark on their own paper. You do not need to be a studio artist. You do need to put the object on the table before the name, and to leave the child’s mark on the child’s page. WELCOME 8 That is enough to begin.1 — Michael Gannotti 1 Access date for locked numbers and program checks in this edition: 24 September 2026. Full citations for studies named in later chapters live in the Notes for those chapters and in end matter. How to use this book this week Pick one looking-and-making move. Run the Art Hour a few times. Leave one crumb on Friday. That is the honest “lesson plan.” Not a 180-day craft calendar. Not a unit binder that never returns to the mug. This week’s shape 1. Choose one chapter focus. Examples: notice before name on a mug or postcard; child’s first mark block; follow-the-edge; two-puddle mix; tear collage; foam stamp; pinch pot; tell-me talk (not “pretty”); a short whosemark check. 2. Run three to five Art Hours of the named shape in The Art Hour (~20– 40 minutes each). Same focus. Fresh object if you can; same mug or leaf revisited if that is what the week holds. 3. Do one in-home try-it from the chapter’s practice section (mug look, fat crayon block, tempera puddle, tear collage, foam stamp, pinch pot, window frame, light/dark water). 4. Do one out-of-home try-it once in the week when you can (museum onework sit, sculpture walk, nature line/texture, library picture-book look first, grocery color cart, architecture edge walk, gallery child choice). Ordinary safety. Adult present outdoors. 5. Friday: one diagnostic pattern + done-enough. Hear one wrong turn without crushing the look — name-first, adult-filled mark, empty pretty loop, coloring-sheet-only week, generated image in the folder. Check whether the child can show the move two ways, and whether a page still feels like theirs after a night. Details live in each chapter’s “done enough” and in the 9 HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 10 assessments chapter. If a day only holds twenty minutes: object + notice + short make + exit crumb. One named move done well beats a rushed craft medley. There is no nationally representative study of art minutes per day in U.S. homes that this book can quote — so there is no honest “required” dose to post on the fridge — and no need to shame a week that held three short sits. Placement by skill (5–7 / 8–10) Use the bands as planning help, not as birthday locks. 5–7 leans look-heavy: fat tools, tear before fancy cut, playdough or air-dry, oral exit, you may scribe the caption they said, process over likeness. 8–10 may take a longer make: blind contour soft, foam print, overlap, written because-I-see crumbs — still refuse MFA critique. If looking habits are weak, stay on 5–7 LOOK and MARK longer, regardless of a ninth birthday. A seven-year-old who can look at a rim and mark it may run early observation moves. A nine-year-old still melting down on long sits needs shorter material play. Soft band placement lives as a try-it shape in the assessments chapter — place by what they can show, not by the cake candles. How to read a teaching chapter Read Why this matters and For the parent first — alone, if you can. Do the five-minute parent warm-up with tomorrow’s object or paper before the child sits. Practice the sentence “What do you notice?” aloud once. Check that the materials are actually on the table, not still in a cupboard. Check the seal (ACMI AP and/or Conforms to ASTM D-4236) before you open a new bottle. Then use How to teach it this week as your script for the table. Exact wording is there on purpose. Use it. Age-band moves for 5–7 and 8–10 live inside that heading. Practice that actually builds learning names try-its with time, materials, mess/safety, the fun, and the skill — at least one inside the home and at least one HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 11 outside. The talk box gives the locked opening question, follow-ups, how to wait, and what a stuck silence usually means. Read For the student with your child, or let them hear it. Warm, direct, short. Never a lecture about research. Use If it isn’t clicking when something stalls. Three diagnostics. No shame. Correct a wrong reason without crushing the look. Rescue order is ask, wait, hint, short demo on demo paper, return the tool. Tools, including AI stays short and points back to the Art…

Inside the chapters you will see two planning bands: 5–7 and 8–10. Place your child by skill, not by birthday. 4 WELCOME 5 A careful six-year-old and a fluent nine-year-old may sit in the same looking move on different days. The focus lock for the whole book is simple: Look before name. Make before polish. Hold that, and the rest of the manual becomes practice. What a good Art Hour looks like Picture a kitchen table. Not a museum field trip every day. Not a silent “color this packet” hour. Not a product chase for the fridge. You put a mug, a leaf, fat crayons, or two tempera puddles on the table. items.text: 1 Art for Young Minds Michael Gannotti A homeschool teaching manual for ages 11–14. Illustrated teaching-manual edition, 27 September 2026. Notes run in one series at the back. Chapter-opening images are original still-lifes, not portraits of people or children. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to use this book this week • If you only remember five things • The Art Hour • Chapter 1 — What art looks like at 11–14 • Chapter 2 — The sketchbook and observational drawing • Chapter 3 — Value, light, and form • Chapter 4 — Space and perspective • Chapter 5 — Color and design • Chapter 6 — Cut, print, and build: tools with rules • Chapter 7 — Looking at real works and the language of critique • Chapter 8 — Portfolio and progress checks • Chapter 9 — Records and next steps • Chapter 10 — Resources • A Note on Sources • Notes 3 Welcome You do not need to be an artist to teach an eleven- to fourteen-year-old to draw what they see. You need an object on the table, one good question, and the patience to wait for the answer. That is what this book is for. A Tuesday, for example It is a little after ten in the morning. A desk lamp is clamped to the kitchen table and pointed at a single egg sitting on a dark dish towel. A twelve-year-old has a sketchbook open to a fresh page and has already written the date in the corner. Her arm is straight out, pencil upright, one eye closed. She is measuring how tall the egg is against how wide. Her father sits across the table with his own cheap sketchbook. He is not drawing well. He is not trying to. He asks one question — “What do you actually see, before either of us decides if it’s good?” — and then he does the hardest thing in this book. He waits. After a long moment she says the shadow is darker right up against the egg than it is farther out. That is true. He hadn’t noticed. Neither had she, until she looked. Twenty minutes later there is a smudgy, honest egg on the page, a one-line note underneath it (“shadow darkest where it touches”), and a pencil back in the jar. That was an Art Hour: about forty minutes, five short beats, a dated page at the end. (That Tuesday is a composite, drawn from common situations. It is not a real family. You will meet a few more like it in this book, always labelled.) The student you actually have Eleven to fourteen is a wonderful and slightly prickly age for art. Your student can work longer than they could at nine. They can hold a project across several days. They want their drawings to look real, and they notice — instantly — when a drawing doesn’t. Many of them are harder on their own page than anyone else will ever be. They are more alert to being watched and judged than they were a few years ago. And their hands are ready for tools that 4 WELCOME 5 were off the table at eight: a charcoal stick, a lino gouge, and, at thirteen or fourteen if your family chooses, a craft knife used under a clear protocol. This is also the age when a great many people decide they “can’t draw.” If you decided that about yourself at about this age, you are in very large company. You are also about to get a second chance, sitting beside your student. Here is the good news, plainly. Most drawing trouble is seeing trouble. Careful research with adults found that the biggest source of drawing mistakes was misjudging what the object actually looked like — not an unsteady hand.1 That was an adult study, so treat it as a useful map rather than a promise. But it points straight at something you can teach: seeing, with simple tools for measuring and checking. The focus of the whole book See before you judge. Sketch before you polish. See before you judge means look, measure, and describe before anyone decides whether something is good — your student’s drawing, a painting in a museum, a sibling’s print, your own ugly page. Judgment still comes. It comes last, and it comes with reasons. Sketch before you polish means thumbnails, quick studies, and honest first pages are the real work, not a warm-up before the real work. The good paper comes out after the sketch has made the decisions. If you used Art for Little Thinkers with a younger child, you will recognize this. Look before name; make before polish has grown up. What you actually do You do not have to demonstrate like a trained artist. Your jobs are ones you can do well starting this week: • Set up the object and the lamp. • Protect the quiet minute of looking. • Ask one good question — each chapter gives you the exact words — and then wait. • Keep your hands off the student’s page. If you demonstrate, do it on a separate sheet. • Teach the tool rules first, and count the tools back in at the end. • Date things and keep them. That is most of assessment and nearly all of record-keeping. Your student does the seeing, sketching, making, and talking. That division of labor is the method, not a shortcut around it. WELCOME 6 Two readers at once Most of this book talks to you, the parent or co-teacher. Each teaching chapter also has a section headed For the student, written directly to your eleven- to fourteen-year-old. Hand it over. It is short, it does not talk down, and it says a few things — your sketchbook is yours; other people’s opinions come when you ask for them — that land better coming from the book than from a parent. Why this matters now In the 2016 national survey of homeschooling families, about half of homeschooled students in grades 6–8 had art as a subject that year — fewer than in the early grades, more than in high school.2 The survey does not say why. It does suggest that middle school is where art often slips quietly off the week. This book is built to keep it on, at a size a busy home can manage: a few Art Hours a week and a ten-minute sketchbook page on the other days. What this book will not do It will not hand you a 180-day plan. You will get a this-week shape, a pacing sketch for the year, and the judgment to choose. It will not sell you a curriculum or rank programs. The resources chapter describes options by fit — your time, your student’s style, your budget — and starts with the library and free museum collections. It will not promise a portfolio by spring, a percentile, or a student who draws like a professional in six weeks. It will not tell you that art makes students smarter at reading or math. A large review of that question, from Harvard’s Project Zero, found no reliable evidence that it does.3 Art is worth teaching for what art teaches: seeing, making, deciding, and talking about images with evidence. It is not a reprint of Art for Little Thinkers (ages 5–10) or Art for Homeschooling (grades 1–12). If you have a younger child, the first is their book. If your fourteen-year-old is heading into highschool credit, the second picks up there. This book teaches eleven to fourteen. It will never treat a generated image as your student’s work. AI appears here as an optional helper for you, under clear rules, explained once in The Art Hour. It will not ask you to put a brand on the transcript. The course line is Art. Encouragement that is specific This week, you can learn to ask one question and wait through the silence after it. Today, your student can draw one object for ten minutes and write the date on the page. That is enough to begin. WELCOME — Michael Gannotti 7 How to use this book this week Read The Art Hour once. It takes about twenty minutes, and it holds the session shape, the talk-box shape, the safety rules, and the AI rules that every later chapter points back to. Then read the parent sections of Chapter 1. Then start. That is the whole on-ramp. You do not need to read the book cover to cover before the first Art Hour, and you do not need to buy anything first. A pencil, a sketchbook, a lamp, and an egg will carry the first two weeks. This week’s shape 1. Pick one focus. In the first week, that is Chapter 1: the ugly page, the blind contour, the silent look, and one baseline drawing you will keep. 2. Run two to four Art Hours of thirty to fifty minutes, using the five beats in The Art Hour. 3. Ten-minute sketchbook page on the other days. One object, ten minutes, date in the corner. 4. One out-of-home try-it this week or next — a sketchbook outing, a library art-book hunt, a museum room. 5. Friday: a short review. The student tabs three pages in the week’s sketchbook (best, most learned, try again). You run one short check from the chapter and look at the “done enough” list. Here is what that looks like in a real week. Treat it as a sample, not an assignment. Day What happens Monday Art Hour: ugly page on purpose, then blind contour of a hand Ten-minute page Art Hour: five-minute silent look at a real work, then the monthly baseline drawing Ten-minute page; library art-book hunt if the week allows Sketchbook review, one check, done-enough list Pocket sketchbook outing, if it fits Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Weekend 8 HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 9 Most chapters take three to six weeks. Some take longer, and that is fine. The tools chapter in particular goes at the speed of the rules. Placement: skill, not birthday Inside every teaching chapter you will see two planning bands: 11–12 and 13–14. The 11–12 moves assume more modeling from you, shorter sits, sentence starters for talk, soft carving blocks before linoleum, and scissors rather than knives. The 13–14 moves assume longer independent work, multi-session projects, two-point perspective, full value range, fuller critique, and writing about art in the student’s own words. Use the bands as a guide, not a lock. A thirteen-year-old who has never drawn from life starts with the 11–12 moves, and there is nothing lost by it. A confident eleven-year-old may take a 13–14 move early. You will see the label ready 12 on moves that some twelve-year-olds are ready for — traditional linoleum with a bench hook and an adult beside them, for instance, or drawing a box in two-point perspective. A “grade 7 art” book is a publisher’s scope. It is not a legal level, and your student is not behind or ahead of it. Coming from Art for Little Thinkers, or from nothing? Both start in the same place: Chapter 1, with a dated baseline drawing. The baseline tells you where to begin far better than a birthday does. How a teaching chapter is built Every teaching chapter uses the same eight headings in the same order, so you always know where to look. • Why this matters — one page on what this unlocks. • For the parent: understand it yourself — the idea in plain words, an everyday picture and a precise one, the “wrong answers” you should learn to hear, and a five-minute warm-up for you alone. • How to teach it this week — the first try-it, exact wording you can use, how to fade your help, when to stop talking, and the band moves. • Practice that actually builds learning — named try-its in the home and outside it, the chapter’s talk box, and one incorrect example to diagnose together. • For the student — a page or two written directly to your student. • If it isn’t clicking — three common snags and the next move for each. • Tools, including AI — short, and pointing back to The Art Hour. • What “done enough” looks like — a checklist before you move on. HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 10 In order, or by need The chapters build on each other, and the order is the one we recommend: seeing and the sketchbook first, then value, then space, then color and design, then cutting and building, then looking and critique, then the portfolio. You can bend it. If drawing confidence is very low, spend longer in Chapters 1 and 2 before value. Looking at real works (Chapter 7) can thread through the whole year — many families spend a few minutes with one painting every week from the start. The progress checks in Chapter 8 begin in the very first month, even though the chapter sits near the end. And the tools chapter always starts with the rules, no matter when you reach it. A year with this book (a sketch, not a schedule) Month Focus Running alo…

items.text: 1 Art Refresh for Adults Michael Gannotti A warm self-study manual for adults coming back to art. Illustrated edition, 29 September 2026. Notes run in one series at the back; the superscript numbers link to them. The images are original still lifes, with no people and no brands. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The Art Refresh Hour • Chapter 1 — What coming back to art looks like • Chapter 2 — Sketchbook, home studio and tools • Chapter 3 — Drawing from observation and life • Chapter 4 — Painting • Chapter 5 — Photography, digital and design • Chapter 6 — Looking at art: history and museums • Chapter 7 — Critique, feedback and your own statement • Chapter 8 — Keeping going: projects, a body of work, showing or sharing • Chapter 9 — Records • Chapter 10 — Resources • A Note on Sources • Notes 3 Welcome Maybe you drew all the time as a kid and then, somewhere around twelve, stopped. Maybe you took art in school, loved it, and haven’t opened a paint box in twenty years. Maybe you’ve said “I can’t draw” so many times it sounds like a fact. Maybe you’ve just retired, and a wish you kept putting off is finally sitting across the table from you. Maybe you have fifteen minutes on a train and a coat pocket that would hold a small notebook. Maybe you’d like to make something at the kitchen table next to your kids instead of just handing them the markers. This book is for all of you, one reader at a time. You’re the learner here. There’s no teacher’s edition and no student section, because you’re both, and that turns out to be a good arrangement. Rust is ordinary If the first page you draw after years away feels clumsy, good. That’s what the first page feels like for nearly everyone who comes back. Rust isn’t a verdict on you. It’s what happens to any skill you set down for a while, and it comes off the way it came on: a little at a time. “Refresh” in this book doesn’t mean proving you were never rusty. It means rebuilding a practice you’ll actually keep. Small enough to survive a busy week. Steady enough that in three months you can lay your first page beside your newest one and see the difference with your own eyes. “I can’t draw” is a starting place Here is the most encouraging true thing I know about adult drawing. Researchers who studied why most adults struggle to draw what they see tested the usual suspects one at a time. Was it the hand not doing what it was told? Hardly at all. Was it misjudging your own drawing as you went? No. The big source of trouble was in how people saw the object in front of them. They drew what they knew about it instead of what was actually there.1 That changes where you start. If you’ve always said “I can’t draw,” the likely truth is that you haven’t yet trained your eye to see shapes, sizes and angles as they really land in front of you. And seeing can be trained. In another study, college students who took a single term of drawing from observation got clearly better at drawing what they saw, while their basic perception tests didn’t change at all.2 They didn’t need special eyes. The skill was in the practice. 4 WELCOME 5 So you can say “I can’t draw” once more, kindly, if you need to. Then put a mug on the table and we’ll look at it together. What an Art Refresh Hour feels like Picture a Wednesday evening. (It’s an illustration, not a real person.) The dishes are done. You clear one end of the kitchen table, turn a lamp so it lights a pear from the side, and leave your phone in the other room. Look. For three minutes you only look. Where’s the darkest part? Where does the pear’s edge slip into shadow? You name one thing you’ll watch for: the shadow side is bigger than I think. Sketch. Five minutes of stamp-sized boxes on a scrap page, three quick tries at the pear: closer, farther, lower. Make. Twenty minutes on the drawing itself, with a pencil, a cheap sketchbook and a timer running. It goes wrong in the middle, the way drawings do. You keep going. Step back. You prop the page against the sugar bowl and walk to the far side of the room. You ask yourself one question: what do I actually see, what was I after, and what’s the one change I’ll try next? You write one line: shadow works; stem too big. File. You date the page and jot the minutes on a strip inside the cover. Thirty-five minutes, one honest page, and a note for tomorrow. That’s the whole thing. Nothing heroic. On a Monday it might be smaller: twelve minutes on the train with a pocket sketchbook, drawing the umbrella folded on the seat opposite, one line at your stop, the date in the corner. On a Saturday it might be larger: an hour at a museum bench with one painting, or a slow still life on a table you can leave set up. Same five steps, different sizes. It’s called the Art Refresh Hour even when it lasts fifteen minutes, and the front of the book teaches it once, so every chapter after that can simply say “run the Hour.” You need less than you think A pencil. A pen that doesn’t smear. A cheap sketchbook, cheap on purpose, so no page feels too good to spoil. A lamp you can aim. Something in front of you to look at, which your house is already full of. That’s the kit for the first month. Paint, a corner studio and outings come later, when you know what you want from them. Chapter 2 helps you set up a small, safe corner without buying much at all, and the resources chapter starts with the library and the free museum day before it mentions anything with a price. WELCOME 6 The line that holds the book together Look long before you judge; sketch before you polish; sign only what you made. Your eye is what you’re training, so give it time before it hands down a verdict. Cheap, fast tries come before the careful piece. Your name goes only on marks and choices that are yours. You’ll meet that line again. It’s short on purpose, so you can carry it. What this book will do It will give you a rhythm: a daily page of ten to fifteen minutes, a longer sit once or twice a week, and an outing when you can manage one. It will teach drawing from observation, painting, photography, digital work and design, looking at art, critique, and the harder trick of keeping going once the first excitement wears off. It will help you set up a corner at home that’s safe and pleasant to work in, and show you how to keep simple, honest records. At every step it will tell you what to try today: on the commute, at the table, in a weekend sit. What this book won’t do It won’t test you for talent. There’s no quiz at the front to sort the artists from everyone else. It won’t promise you’ll draw like a master in thirty days. If you practice most days, you’ll see real progress in weeks, and that’s a better promise because it’s true. It won’t tell you art will make you smarter or treat an illness. Chapter 1 says plainly, and carefully, what art can and can’t be counted on to do. It won’t sell you a course, rank products, or push a brand. The resources chapter sorts options by fit and starts with what’s free. It won’t hand you a certificate or invent a course credit. The records in Chapter 9 are honest ones a stranger could read. It won’t treat a generated image as your work. And it won’t repeat the books that came before it. This is the fourth and final title in the Art Hour family, after Art for Little Thinkers, Art for Young Minds and Art for Emerging Adults, which teach children and teens with a parent at the table. If you make art with kids, the resources chapter points you to them. This one is yours. Where to begin Read How to Use This Book This Week next. It’s short, and it gets you started. Then the five things, then The Art Refresh Hour, then Chapter 1. Tonight, find a pencil, any paper, and a mug. Tomorrow, write the date in the corner of the page. WELCOME That’s enough to begin. — Michael Gannotti 7 How to Use This Book This Week Start with this week, not the whole book. You don’t need to read every chapter before you draw a line. You need a pencil, a few pockets of time, and the five steps below. This week, in five steps 1. The baseline page. One sitting of about thirty minutes: ten minutes each drawing a mug, your non-drawing hand, and a corner of the room. Date it. No erasing. Then put it away and leave it alone. It isn’t a test. It’s the “before” photo you’ll be glad of in twelve weeks, when you draw the same three things again. Chapter 1 gives you the full try-it.3 2. The why card. An index card and ten minutes. One line: why art, and why now. A second line: what a good month would look like. Tape it inside your sketchbook’s front cover and reread it on the week that goes badly. 3. Daily pages, most days. Ten to fifteen minutes, dated, one thing in front of you, one line of writing underneath. Tie it to something you already do every day, like the first coffee, the train, or the ten minutes after dinner. A missed day is just a missed day. It doesn’t reset anything.4 4. One desk sit. Twenty-five to forty minutes at a table, with a try-it from Chapter 2 or Chapter 3: nine small thumbnails before a drawing, or a chair drawn only by the empty shapes between its legs. 5. One deep sit or outing. Forty-five to seventy-five minutes somewhere with room to settle: one room of a museum with a pencil, a drop-in class, an open drawing session, or an unhurried study at home on a table you can leave set up. At the end of the week, flip through what you made and write one line on your practice strip, the running log you’ll keep inside the sketchbook cover. That’s week one. It’s allowed to be lopsided. A week with the baseline page and two daily pages in it is a real week. Where to start: place by the page, not by age Once the baseline page has sat for a day, take it out and look at it with a friendly eye. It will tell you where to go after Chapters 1 and 2, which set up the rhythm and the corner for everyone. 8 HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 9 • If proportions wobble, the mug leans, the fingers all come out the same length, or the corner of the room tips like a ship’s deck, spend real time on the looking moves in Chapter 3. That’s where most of the fastest gains are. • If the drawing is fairly solid, move through Chapter 3 briskly and on to value and paint in Chapter 4. • If you already have a stack of finished pieces and want to do something with them, Chapter 7 (critique and your own statement) and Chapter 8 (projects, a body of work, showing or sharing) are ready for you. Picture two readers. (Illustrations, not real people.) A retired engineer measures beautifully and has never been told she can draw; her baseline mug is exact and stiff. She can head straight for value and perspective, and learn to loosen up with fast gesture. An art-school graduate who hasn’t drawn in twelve years finds his baseline shaky and frustrating. He may start with a month of daily pages before he touches paint. Same Hour. Different targets. Your age isn’t a placement. Neither is your diploma, or the art grade you got in seventh grade. The page is. The three bands Every chapter offers its work in three sizes, named for where adults actually find time, not for anyone’s age. • Commute or lunch (about 15–20 minutes): a pocket sketchbook on the train, a parked car at lunch, a bench outside the break room. • Desk or shift (about 25–40 minutes): the kitchen table after work, a desk at lunch, a corner studio. • Weekend deep sit (about 45–75 minutes): a table you can leave set up, a museum, an open figure session, a community studio. A retiree may live mostly in deep sits. A parent of toddlers may live in fifteen-minute sessions for a year. Both are doing the book. How each teaching chapter is built Chapters 1 through 8 use the same seven headings, in the same order, so you always know where you are. • Why this matters: what this part of practice opens up for you. • Understand it yourself: the idea in plain words, an everyday picture and a precise one, the wrong turns you’ll hear (including from y…

chapters.text: Resources • A Note on Sources • Notes 3 Welcome Maybe you drew all the time as a kid and then, somewhere around twelve, stopped. Maybe you took art in school, loved it, and haven’t opened a paint box in twenty years. Maybe you’ve said “I can’t draw” so many times it sounds like a fact. Maybe you’ve just retired, and a wish you kept putting off is finally sitting across the table from you. Maybe you have fifteen minutes on a train and a coat pocket that would hold a small notebook. Maybe you’d like to make something at the kitchen table next to your kids instead of just handing them the markers. This book is for all of you, one reader at a time. You’re the learner here. There’s no teacher’s edition and no student section, because you’re both, and that turns out to be a good arrangement. Rust is ordinary If the first page you draw after years away feels clumsy, good. That’s what the first page feels like for nearly everyone who comes back. Rust isn’t a verdict on you. It’s what happens to any skill you set down for a while, and it comes off the way it came on: a little at a time. “Refresh” in this book doesn’t mean proving you were never rusty. It means rebuilding a practice you’ll actually keep. Small enough to survive a busy week. Steady enough that in three months you can lay your first page beside your newest one and see the difference with your own eyes. “I can’t draw” is a starting place Here is the most encouraging true thing I know about adult drawing. Researchers who studied why most adults struggle to draw what they see tested the usual suspects one at a time. Was it the hand not doing what it was told? Hardly at all. Was it misjudging your own drawing as you went? No. The big source of trouble was in how people saw the object in front of them. They drew what they knew about it instead of what was actually there.1 That changes where you start. If you’ve always said “I can’t draw,” the likely truth is that you haven’t yet trained your eye to see shapes, size…

items.summary: Performance is not learning. This teaching-manual is the hour at the table after a fluent model can finish a page in seconds. Chat, tutor, adaptive system, and agent are four jobs. A tool fine at 17 can be wrong at 8. The student still does the work the window cannot keep.
