items.text: History for Homeschooling Michael Gannotti 1 Figure 1: Cover History for Homeschooling Michael Gannotti This illustrated edition is the teaching-manual of 31 August 2026. Endnotes run in one series. Chapter-opening images are original still-lifes, not portraits of persons or children. Documents still constrain the facts. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The History Hour • Chapter 1 — Grades 1–2: Then and now: pictures before dates • Chapter 2 — Grades 3–5: Timeline as a tool: state, early U.S., a source on the table • Chapter 3 — Grades 6–8: World moves and U.S. moves: a period, two accounts, a paragraph • Chapter 4 — World History • Chapter 5 — U.S. History • Chapter 6 — Government / Civics • Chapter 7 — Sources and discussion • Chapter 8 — Geography and the present • Chapter 9 — Records • Chapter 10 — Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome This book exists because the history hour at your table is the whole program. There is no department down the hall and no specialist waiting after lunch. There is you, a student, and today’s year — a story to tell, a source to look at, a question worth waiting for. That is enough, if you know what to do with the hour. I wrote this for a capable, busy, willing parent. You may be teaching two ages at once. You may be fitting history between a job, a toddler, and a grocery run. You may have loved school history, or you may remember it as a fog of dates and names. Many adults feel rusty around dates and names when they sit down to teach. That feeling is common. It is not a verdict. We will move on from it. This book will make you fluent enough in this week’s idea to notice a wrong story and ask a good question — without taking over the talking. You do not need to be a historian. You do need to understand this week’s idea well enough to hear “the book said it, so it happened that way” as one account treated as the only one, not as a finished thought. You need a session shape you can run on a Tuesday. You need a few sentences that actually help. That is the job. A path through history — from first-grade then-and-now stories through a college-ready high-school sequence in world, United States, and civics — is possible at a kitchen table. The path is not a personality trait and it is not a percentile. It is a sequence of ideas, practiced until they hold, with you in the chair. About 3.4 percent of U.S. students ages 5–17 were homeschooled in 2022–23 — roughly 1.765 million children.1 That figure is context, not a ranking. You are 1 Ellena Sempeles and Jiashan Cui, Parent and Family Involvement in Education: 2023, NCES 2024-113 (Washington, DC: National Center for Education Statistics, September 2024), Table A-6: 3.4 percent homeschooled, approximately 1,765,000 students, ages 5–17 with a K–12 grade equivalent, 2022–23. https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2024/2024113.pdf. Access date for URLs in these notes: 31 August 2026. Latest federal count this book uses; not a 2026 national total. A neighboring 5.2 4 WELCOME 5 one of those tables. Homeschooling is legal in all fifty states and the District of Columbia. The paperwork is not one load: Texas asks almost nothing of the state agency; New York asks for a written plan and regular reports.2 There is no national homeschool diploma and no national history credit a registrar already files.3 In the last federal tables that published the row, most homeschool families were already teaching social studies that year — 78 percent overall, 81 percent in grades 9–12.4 The titles that travel — Social Studies, U.S. History, World History, Government, Civics, Geography, Economics — are names a stranger can read. The hour in front of you is the work. What a good history hour looks like You sit down already knowing today’s idea. A picture, a map, or a short document is on the table, with the maker visible. You tell a short story — one named person in a named place — then you stop. The child looks. You ask one good question — not “what year was it?” but “who made this, and what did they want us to believe?” Then you wait. Three seconds feels long. It is the work. Practice mixes the new percent received instruction at home (homeschooled or full-time virtual) and is a different bucket. 2 Texas Education Agency, “Home Schooling,” https://tea.texas.gov/families-andstudents/finding-school-your-child/home-schooling. New York State Education Department, “Home Instruction Questions and Answers,” https://www.nysed.gov/nonpublic-schools/homeinstruction-questions-and-answers. Homeschooling is legal in all fifty states and D.C.; these two pages illustrate a light-process and a heavier-process pattern, not a national template. This book is not legal advice. 3 Texas Education Agency, “Home Schooling”: “The State of Texas does not award a diploma to students that are home schooled.” New York State Education Department, “Home Instruction Questions and Answers”: a high school diploma “may only be awarded to a student enrolled in a registered secondary school.” North Carolina Division of Non-Public Education, “Home School Records Retention & Diplomas FAQs,” https://www.doa.nc.gov/divisions/non-public-education/home-schools/faqs/recordsretention-diplomas: the State does not issue a diploma or a transcript; the home-school chief administrator does. NCAA Eligibility Center, Home School Toolkit 2025–26, http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/eligibility_center/Student_Resources/Home_School_Toolkit.pdf, treats proof of graduation as a family- or umbrella-issued artifact. 4 Jiashan Cui and Rachel Hanson, Homeschooling in the United States: Results from the 2012 and 2016 Parent and Family Involvement Survey, NCES 2020-001 (Washington, DC: National Center for Education Statistics, 2019), Table 9: among K–12-equivalent homeschoolers, 78 percent were being taught “social science, history, social studies” that year (81 percent in grades 9–12). Geography that year: 41 percent overall. The 2023 First Look did not republish the subject-taught tables. https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2020/2020001.pdf. WELCOME 6 looking with last week’s story. The hour ends with one short task they do alone: a spoken sentence, a caption, a claim that points at the source. You stop talking sooner than feels polite. The child looks and talks. You hold the key. That is the hour. The next long piece of this front matter, The History Hour, will teach it in full. Later chapters will not reinvent it. Figure 2: A kitchen-table history hour Stories first, then the question. A date list is not a year. Historical looking does not spring from age or from being “good at history”; it goes against the grain of how we ordinarily think.5 The chapters will give you wording. The hour will stay this shape. 5 Sam Wineburg, “Historical Thinking and Other Unnatural Acts,” Phi Delta Kappan 80, no. 7 (1999): 488–99: historical thinking “in its deepest forms, is neither a natural process nor something that springs automatically from psychological development”; its achievement “actually goes against the grain of how we ordinarily think.” “It is much easier to learn names, dates, and stories than it is to change the fundamental mental structures that we use to grasp the meaning of the past.” WELCOME 7 What you will actually get Each teaching chapter does eight jobs, always in the same order, so you are never hunting for the move. You will learn why this week’s idea is worth the struggle — what it unlocks later. You will understand the idea yourself, in plain language, with one everyday picture and one precise picture, and with the wrong stories you should be able to hear. You will get a session you can run this week, including exact wording, named activities, and a discussion box with this week’s questions. You will get practice that builds learning, not a slog of coverage. Your student will get a short section of their own. If it isn’t clicking, you will get three diagnostics and a next move for each, with no shame in the room. Tools, including AI, stay optional and adult-side. And you will get a plain checklist for “done enough,” so you can place by skill rather than by birthday. The eight teaching chapters follow the work, not twelve thin grade labels: thenand-now in grades 1–2; state and early U.S. stories, with a timeline as a tool, in grades 3–5; world moves and U.S. moves in grades 6–8; then high-school World History, U.S. History, civics, sources and discussion, and geography and the present. Records and resources come last. This week you can learn the session shape and today’s idea well enough to hear a wrong story. Today the child can look at one picture or one short source and say something true about it without you filling the silence. What this book will not do This book will not hand you 180 days of coverage. A year of photocopies is not a teaching method, and I will not pretend it is. Coverage is a map. Depth is the hour. It will not sell you a curriculum. Later, a short resources chapter names common programs by fit — parent load, narrative versus textbook versus document-heavy, religious versus secular, how they place a student — so you can choose. Story of the World, Tapestry of Grace, Notgrass, All American History, a textbook path, and Digital Inquiry Group’s Reading Like a Historian lessons are tools. None of them is this book, and this book is not a catalog in disguise. A family may combine. Combining does not turn a brand into a course name. The transcript still WELCOME 8 says World History or U.S. History. It will not promise a score. There is no guaranteed percentile, no guaranteed AP number, no guaranteed NAEP bar, and no guaranteed college letter inside these pages. What this book can promise is a path: the ideas in order, at the skill the child actually has, until they can do the next idea unaided. NAEP Proficient is not “on grade level,” and there is no national homeschool history score in these pages to wave.6 It is not a Common Core tract, for or against. The C3 Framework is an inquiry map states may use; it is not a grade-by-grade content list and it is not a homeschool mandate.7 California, Texas, and Virginia print their own maps, and they do not agree about when the world year happens. A publisher’s “grade 6” book is a scope, not a legal grade. Ancient civilizations in sixth grade is California’s sequence, not a national rule. It is not a culture-war pamphlet. Teach the year on the table. Name a live debate in one sentence when it is load-bearing, then teach. A path through history is the promise. A culture-war win is not. History does not automatically mint a citizen.8 If civics is the aim, teach civics, and point to Publius for a Federalist week. And this is not a sequel. Publius and Critical Thinking for Life are other books. If 6 National Center for Education Statistics, “Fast Facts: U.S. History and Civics (1160),” https://nces.ed.gov/fastfacts/display.asp?id=1160: grade 8 U.S. history, 2022, average 258; 13 percent at or above NAEP Proficient; 60 percent at or above NAEP Basic. NCES states that “the NAEP Proficient achievement level does not represent grade level proficiency as determined by other assessment standards.” NCES does not publish a nationally representative homeschool NAEP U.S. history score. 7 National Council for the Social Studies, The College, Career, and Civic Life (C3) Framework for Social Studies State Standards (Silver Spring, MD: NCSS, 2013), https://www.socialstudies.org/sites/default/files/c3/C3-Framework-for-Social-Studies.pdf: the Framework “intentionally preserves the critical choices around the selection of curricular content taught at each grade level as a decision best made by each state.” It does not assign ancient civilizations to grade 6. California History–Social Science Content Standards (State Board adoption 9 October 1998; CDE Press 2000): World History and Geography: Ancient Civilizations is the grade 6 course. https://www.cde.ca.gov/be/st/ss/documents/histsocscistnd.pdf. 8 Marjolein Wi…

items.text: History for Little Thinkers Michael Gannotti 1 Figure 1: Cover History for Little Thinkers Michael Gannotti This illustrated edition is the teaching-manual of 13 September 2026. Endnotes run in one series. Chapter-opening images are original still-lifes, not portraits of persons or children. Documents still constrain the facts. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The History Hour • Chapter 1 — What history looks like at 5–10 • Chapter 2 — Objects, pictures, and “who made this” • Chapter 3 — Family and community oral history • Chapter 4 — Maps as pictures and place • Chapter 5 — Timeline light • Chapter 6 — Holidays and commemorations with care • Chapter 7 — Talking and writing history • Chapter 8 — Short assessments and progress checks • Chapter 9 — Records • Chapter 10 — Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome You do not need a history degree to teach a five- to ten-year-old real history looking. You need a piece from then on the table before the story, and one good question you are willing to wait for. That is what this book is for. Why this book exists Many adults remember history as a list of names and dates. That memory can leave you feeling rusty when a child asks what happened long ago. Feeling rusty is normal. It is not a character flaw. At ages 5–10, history looking does not begin with a wall of centuries. It begins with pictures, objects, and talk. A child can sort then from now by what is in a picture. A child can name what they notice on a ticket, a coin, or a family photograph. A child can ask who made this before anyone reads the caption. A child can hang three pictures in order and say what happened first. Those moves are not a waiting room for middle school. They are the work. This book teaches you how to run a short History Hour at home — roughly twenty to forty minutes — with a piece from then before the story, and with who made this before the body of any text. Inside the chapters you will see two planning bands: 5–7 and 8–10. Place your child by skill, not by birthday. A fluent eightyear-old and a careful six-year-old may sit in the same looking move on different days. The focus lock for the whole book is simple: 4 WELCOME 5 Piece-from-then before story. Who made this. Hold that, and the rest of the manual becomes practice. What a good History Hour looks like Picture a kitchen table. Not a museum field trip every day. Not a silent “read the chapter” hour. Not an app chase. You put one object or photograph down. You cover the caption for a minute if you need to. You ask what the child sees that tells them this is then — or what tells them this is now. You wait. You ask who made this, or who is in the picture, and you wait again. Then you tell a short story the piece can carry. Then the child tries one small thing: a sort, a drawing, a label, a retell. Then they leave one exit crumb — one spoken sentence, one sticky, one sorted pile named. That is the hour. Library visits and museum days motivate. They do not replace the looking move on the table. You will meet the full session shape in The History Hour. Later chapters point back to it. You do not rebuild the spine every week. Two readers at once This is a teaching manual for the parent or co-teacher at the table, with short student sections a child can actually use. When you read a parent section, you are learning today’s looking move well enough to hear a wrong turn — a year-first question, a “they were just stupid” jab, a shiny thing sorted as “then,” a generated diary filed as a real primary, a holiday recitation with no finger on the picture, an encyclopedia lecture with no piece on the table. You learn what to say next without grabbing the answer or filling the silence with the story. When your child reads (or hears) a student section, they get respect. No baby-talk. No lecture about you. They get a tiny worked example, two tries, and a chance to explain it back. WELCOME 6 What this book will not do It will not hand you a 180-day worksheet dump. It will not sell you a curriculum, crown one program, or promise a score. It will not reprint History for Homeschooling — that book serves grades 1–12, with later survey and transcript edges. For that map, see that book once. This book teaches the 5–10 History Hour. It is not a sequel to Critical Thinking Skills for Little Thinkers or English for Little Thinkers. One pointer each is enough. Then we teach history as looking. It will not title your subject Little Thinkers History I. A stranger-readable title is History or Social Studies. It will not turn the hour into a culture-war pamphlet. Safe history objects only: a coin, a ticket, a tool, a family photograph with permission, a library postcard, a museum reproduction labelled as such, a hand-drawn neighborhood map, a clothesline of then/now pictures, a holiday object handled with care, a dated notebook. It will not ask you to wait until middle school to begin. Children this age can look. They do not become historians because someone bought a timeline poster. How the book is built Front matter tells you how to use the week, five things to remember, and the History Hour once — including the AI box for ages 5–10, said carefully and only once. Eight teaching chapters follow: what history looks like at 5–10; objects, pictures, and who made this; family and community oral history; maps as pictures; timeline light; holidays with care; talking and writing history; short assessments and progress checks. Then records and resources. Records keep a dated notebook, a retell, a who-madethis check, and a then/now sort under History / Social Studies. Resources name common programs by fit — parent load, style, placement, cost shape — with library and museum first. Fit, not rank. Every teaching chapter uses the same eight headings, a talk box with an exact open- WELCOME 7 ing question, named try-its inside the home and outside it, and age-band moves for 5–7 and 8–10. Encouragement that is specific This week you can learn one looking move well enough to hear a year-first question and turn it back to the picture. Today your child can point at one thing in a picture and say what they notice. You do not need to be a historian. You do need to put a piece on the table before the story, and to ask who made this. That is enough to begin. — Michael Gannotti How to use this book this week Pick one looking move. Run the History Hour a few times. Leave one crumb on Friday. That is the honest “lesson plan.” Not a 180-day calendar. Not a unit binder that never returns to the piece. This week’s shape 1. Choose one chapter focus. Examples: then/now from what is in the picture; who made this on a photo; one relative’s one-event story with consent; a walk drawn badly as a map; three pictures on a string; a holiday object with care; a caption that could only come from looking. 2. Run three to five History Hours of the named shape in The History Hour (~20–40 minutes each). Same focus. Fresh piece if you can; same piece revisited if that is what the week holds. 3. Do one in-home try-it from the chapter’s practice section (coin, photo before caption, ticket, tool, kitchen memory with consent, then/now shoes, three-pile sort, object label). 4. Do one out-of-home try-it once in the week when you can (library photo hunt, museum one thing, plaque read, thrift mystery, street then clues). Ordinary safety. No cold quiz of strangers for “oral history.” 5. Friday: one diagnostic wrong + done-enough. Hear one wrong reason without crushing the look. Check whether the child can show the move two ways, and whether it holds after a night. Details live in each chapter’s “done enough” and in the assessments chapter. If a day only holds twenty minutes: piece + who-made-this + exit crumb. One named move done well beats a rushed medley. There is no nationally representa8 HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 9 tive study of history minutes per day in U.S. homes that this book can quote — so there is no honest “required” dose to post on the fridge — and no need to shame a week that held three short sits. How to read a teaching chapter Read Why this matters and For the parent first — alone, if you can. Do the five-minute parent warm-up with tomorrow’s piece before the child sits. Practice the sentence “Who made this?” aloud once. Check that a credit line or maker clue is ready, or that you will label a reproduction honestly. Then use How to teach it this week as your script for the table. Exact wording is there on purpose. Use it. Age-band moves for 5–7 and 8–10 live inside that heading. Practice that actually builds learning names try-its with time, materials, safety, the fun, and the skill — at least one inside the home and at least one outside. The talk box gives the locked opening question, follow-ups, how to wait, and what a stuck silence usually means. Read For the student with your child, or let them hear it. Warm, direct, short. Never a lecture about research. Use If it isn’t clicking when something stalls. Three diagnostics. No shame. Correct a wrong reason without crushing the look. Tools, including AI stays short and points back to the History Hour AI box. Do not rebuild policy every chapter. What “done enough” looks like is your leave-this-chapter checklist. Placement by skill, not birthday. A publisher’s “grade 2 history workbook” is a scope, not a legal grade, and not a transcript line. Sibling and mixed-age homes Share the piece. Split the try. The younger child may draw, sort, or say one then-clue and one now-clue. The older child may cover the body until who-when-why is said, write a caption, or lightly check two pieces on the same small topic. HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 10 Give each child a turn to speak. After one answers, wait so the next can add — not so the older becomes unpaid tutor as their only role. They need their own looking move too. Multilingual homes Looking works in the family’s talk language. Who-made-this and Observe work before English labels arrive. When print is in another script, you read the attribution aloud; the child still sources by hearing who wrote or made it. Do not delay History Hour until decoding is “ready.” Looking is not decoding. Activity banks are a menu Later chapters pull named try-its from banks (objects, oral history, maps, timeline light, then/now, holidays, talk, write, outings, ask-the-source). A chapter picks a few. It does not assign all seventy-three. Coverage itch is the enemy of looking. What to skip for now Skip chapters you are not ready to teach this month. The map is a path, not a race. Skip vendor shopping until you have run a few Hours with free pieces: a family photo with permission, a coin, a library postcard, a print from a public archive with a credit line. Skip AI tools until you have read the History Hour AI box once. The child looks. You may use a tool on your account. The child does not sit alone with an open chat. Records without drama Keep a dated notebook. Title the work History or Social Studies. Note the piece, the who-made-this check, a short retell, and a then/now sort when you do one. HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 11 That file is enough for most elementary weeks. The records chapter comes later. Never brand the subject line. Never Little Thinkers History I. One week, then another After Friday’s crumb, choose next week’s focus. Revisit yesterday’s piece sometimes. Mix last week’s then/now into a warm-up. Stop while a look remains. You will understand this week’s move. You will know what to say tomorrow. You can do this. If you only remember five things Keep this page short. Pin it where you plan the week. When the hour feels scattered, return here before you add more materials. 1. Piece-from-then before story Put the object, photograph, coin, ticket, or labelled reproduction on the table first. Looking is the lesson. The summary story waits. A fluent adult lecture with no piece is not a History Hour. Library and museum days…

chapters.text: Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome You do not need a history degree to teach a five- to ten-year-old real history looking. You need a piece from then on the table before the story, and one good question you are willing to wait for. That is what this book is for. Why this book exists Many adults remember history as a list of names and dates. That memory can leave you feeling rusty when a child asks what happened long ago. Feeling rusty is normal. It is not a character flaw. At ages 5–10, history looking does not begin with a wall of centuries. It begins with pictures, objects, and talk. A child can sort then from now by what is in a picture. A child can name what they notice on a ticket, a coin, or a family photograph. A child can ask who made this before anyone reads the caption. A child can hang three pictures in order and say what happened first. Those moves are not a waiting room for middle school. They are the work. This book teaches you how to run a short History Hour at home — roughly twenty to forty minutes — with a piece from then before the story, and with who made this before the body of any text. Inside the chapters you will see two planning bands: 5–7 and 8–10. Place your child by skill, not by birthday. A fluent eightyear-old and a careful six-year-old may sit in the same looking move on different days. The focus lock for the whole book is simple: 4 WELCOME 5 Piece-from-then before story. Who made this. Hold that, and the rest of the manual becomes practice. What a good History Hour looks like Picture a kitchen table. Not a museum field trip every day. Not a silent “read the chapter” hour. Not an app chase. You put one object or photograph down. You cover the caption for a minute if you need to. You ask what the child sees that tells them this is then — or what tells them this is now. You wait. You ask who made this, or who is in the picture, and you wait again. Then you tell a short story the piece can carry. Then the child tries one small thing:…

items.text: History for Young Minds Michael Gannotti 1 Figure 1: Cover History for Young Minds Michael Gannotti This illustrated edition is the teaching-manual of 13 September 2026. Endnotes run in one series. Chapter-opening images are original still-lifes, not portraits of persons or children. Documents still constrain the facts. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The History Hour • Chapter 1 — What history looks like at 11–14 • Chapter 2 — Reading a source • Chapter 3 — Two sources and corroboration • Chapter 4 — Context without drowning • Chapter 5 — Early civic texts gently • Chapter 6 — Maps, timelines, and place • Chapter 7 — Talking and writing history • Chapter 8 — Short assessments and progress checks • Chapter 9 — Records • Chapter 10 — Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome You are holding a how-to for teaching history at home with ages 11–14. The aim is simple. Put a named source on the table before the tidy summary story. Ask who made it, when, and for whom. Let your adolescent look and talk. You ask one good question and wait. That is the spine of this book: source before summary, with early civic texts treated gently as documents, not slogans. You do not need to be a historian. You do need to hear a summary-first answer, a textbook-as-the-facts answer, a year-first quiz, a birthday gate (“wait until high school”), and a model summary parked where a credited piece should sit — and to ask a better question without grabbing the answer or filling the silence with the story. Who this book is for Two readers at once. You, the parent or co-teacher at the table: busy, willing, and often a little rusty on names and dates. That rust is normal. Many adults were taught history as a list to memorize. This book makes you fluent enough in today’s looking move to run a short History Hour well — and to hear a wrong turn without turning the table into a fight. Your student, ages 11–14: a person, not a percentile. They get short, respectful sections they can actually use. Never baby-talk. Never a lecture about their parents. At 11–12, they can cover the body until who-when-why is said, run Observe→Reflect→Question with purpose emerging, lightly compare two 4 WELCOME 5 short accounts, interrupt presentism with a their-world prompt, treat one short civic excerpt as a document with a maker, and write a spoken or one-sentence claim that points at a named source. They can use a map or timeline under a story they already own. At 13–14, they add audience and purpose more clearly, name limitations across kinds of sources, organize evidence for a short claim paragraph, compare accounts that answer different questions, and pair a grievance shape with a constitutional limit gently — still without a Constitution-chain march. They can ask who is missing from the record. Place by skill, not birthday. A thirteen-year-old who still jumps to the summary may need the 11–12 scaffolds. An eleven-year-old who already sources before the body may take the next try. The work lives in the home and outside it: credited excerpt on the table, library primary hunt, museum one object, courthouse or plaque read, archive screen with an adult. What a good History Hour looks like Picture this. A credited short excerpt sits on the table — a letter header, a diary day, a newspaper masthead, a soft period image, one civic clause. The body may be covered at first. Your student names maker, date, and type from the credit line. Then they look: Observe, Reflect, Question. You give a tiny bit of background — enough for the piece to make sense, not an encyclopedia tour. You ask one authentic question. You wait. They try. You end with a short exit ticket: one sourcing sentence, or (at 13–14) a short claim that names the source. That session runs about 25–45 minutes. Coverage is a map; depth is the hour. One named move done well beats a rushed medley. Shared looking, kitchen talk, and outings motivate. They do not replace the source-before-summary looking move. This is not a 180-day worksheet dump. It is not a culture-war pamphlet. It is not a high-school Document-Based Lesson packet every week. Library and museum visits belong here — they supply real pieces and real places. The looking still happens on a named source. WELCOME 6 Focus lock Two promises, held for the whole book: 1. Source before summary. Attribution before the body. The credit line is part of the look. A fluent summary from a machine is performance, not the adolescent’s looking. A generated diary is not a primary. 2. Early civic texts gently. Magna Carta, the Declaration, the Constitution (and compact, charter, amendment edges) appear as document edges — one clause, source card, then-words — not as a campaign speech and not as a forced march through a founding chain. Everything else in these chapters serves those two locks: two accounts and light corroboration, context without drowning, maps and timelines as tools under owned stories, claim plus named source, short kitchen skill checks. Safe objects only: a credited short excerpt, a newspaper voice with an honesty card, a diary day (honest excerpt), a soft political cartoon, a speech excerpt, a ship manifest or list kept soft, an image pair of the same event, a civic clause with maker and date, a period map, an owned-story timeline, a dated notebook. Soft entry on hard past. Graphic violence is not the default piece box. What this book will not do It will not sell you a curriculum. It will not promise a score or a percentile. It will not hand you a year of worksheets. It will not reprint History for Little Thinkers (ages 5–10 piece-from-then / who-made-this) with longer words — no Coin Clues, Kitchen Memory, or then/now clothesline scripts dressed up for middle grades. It will not reprint History for Homeschooling (grades 1–12 surveys, transcript export, AP/CLEP edges). One pointer each, then teach 11–14 history. It is not a sequel to Critical Thinking for Young Minds or English for Young Minds. One pointer each, then teach history as looking at a named source. It will not title your subject Young Minds History I. A stranger-readable record says History or Social Studies. It will not dump a Constitution chain as the civic week (that deeper civic work lives elsewhere). It will not treat a generated diary as a primary, or a model summary as the source on the table. It will not invent a ninth teaching chapter called “life of the habit” — that rhythm lives in the History Hour, in done-enough checklists, and in the records you keep. WELCOME 7 How the book is built Front matter once: this welcome, how to use the book this week, five things to remember, and the History Hour (session shape, talk-box shape, in-home and out-of-home try-it shape, and the AI box once for ages 11–14). Eight teaching chapters, each with the same eight headings: why it matters; for the parent; how to teach it this week; practice that builds learning; for the student; if it isn’t clicking; tools including AI; what “done enough” looks like. Every teaching chapter has a talk box with a locked opening question, follow-ups, wait, and stucksilence notes. Named try-its live in the home and outside it. Then records and resources: what to keep under a stranger-readable title, and programs by fit — library and museum first — without crowning a winner. Encouragement for this week Parent: learn to put the attribution card down before the story. Practice who-whenwhy alone for five minutes with tomorrow’s piece. Cut civic excerpts to size before you sit down. Student: cover the body until you can say who made this, when, and for whom — then look. You are allowed to wait. You may change your mind when you look again. You can do this. The piece is on the table. The summary can wait. How to use this book this week This book is a menu of looking moves, not a calendar you must finish. Pick one focus. Run a few short hours. Check what stuck. Move on when the skill holds — not when the birthday says so. One focus, one week 1. Name one focus move from the chapter you are in. Examples: attribution before the body; Observe→Reflect→Question on a credit line; two short accounts without “one must be lying”; one civic clause as a document; a claim that names a source. 2. Schedule three to five History Hours of the named shape (~25–45 minutes each). You do not need five every week. Three solid hours beat five rushed ones. 3. Pick one in-home try-it and one out-of-home try-it from that chapter (or from the History Hour shapes). Time, materials, safety, the fun, and the skill are named so you can run them without inventing a field trip from scratch. 4. Friday (or your last hour): one diagnostic wrong answer you can hear, plus the “done enough” checklist from the chapter. Source a claim, corroborate two sources, or write a short argument when those are the week’s skills — kitchen checks, not a percentile battery. That is the honest “lesson plan.” Not 180 worksheets. Not a NAEP panic. Not a brand name on a transcript line. 8 HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 9 How to open a chapter Read Why this matters and For the parent first — alone, before you sit with your student. Do the parent warm-up (five to eight minutes with tomorrow’s piece). Then teach from How to teach it this week and Practice. Hand your student the For the student pages when they are ready to try. Use If it isn’t clicking when a wrong reason shows up. Point back to the History Hour AI box from Tools; do not invent a new AI policy every chapter. End with What “done enough” looks like before you advance. Sibling and mixed-age notes Share the piece. Split the try. A younger sibling who still lives in History for Little Thinkers grain (piece-fromthen, who-made-this, oral retell) can look at the same object with a shorter ask: what do you notice; who might have made this; one wonder. Your 11–14 student runs the full source card, Observe→Reflect→Question, and the exit ticket for this book. Do not force the younger child into a claim paragraph. Do not shrink the older student’s hour into a then/now clothesline. If two adolescents sit at different bands, give both the same credited piece. Let the 11–12 student exit with a sourcing sentence. Let the 13–14 student add a limitation or a short claim paragraph. One table. Two exits. Multilingual and hard-prose notes Looking works in the family’s talk language. When archaic English blocks the look, the adult reads the attribution aloud and scaffolds one hard sentence — that is access, not rescue of the thinking. Then return eyes to the credit line and the piece. Do not replace today’s looking lesson with a full English morphology hour. Point once to English for Young Minds if print stamina is the real blocker, then come back to history looking. HOW TO USE THIS BOOK THIS WEEK 10 What to have on the table • One credited short excerpt or image (library printout, textbook primary page, public-domain civic clause, museum postcard). • An attribution / honesty card (maker, date, type, original / excerpt / translation / reproduction). • Sticky notes or a simple notebook line for Observe / Reflect / Question and the exit ticket. • Optional: a second short account for corroboration weeks; a period map or owned-story timeline card when place or time is the focus. You do not need a wall of posters. You do not need a generated “colonial diary.” You need a named piece and a question. When to slow down or go ahead Slow down when the student still narrates the year before anyone has looked at the credit line, treats the textbook as “the facts,” or freezes because the question was year-first. Stay on source-before-summary until attribution is said without shame. Go ahead when they can name maker, date, and type from the credit line on a fresh piece, point at a line when asked how they know, and write (or say) a claim that names the source. Birthday is not the gate. Skill is. Records this week Date the notebook. Name the source. Write one…

items.title: History Refresh for Adults
items.summary: Usable civic literacy is ordinary adult work: a feed card, a ballot pamphlet, a plaque, a short civic excerpt with a credit line. A working adult who is not a historian can run that hour on a train or after the kids are in bed — if a caption is not allowed to pass as the event, and a model précis is not allowed to pass as a primary.

Documents still constrain the facts. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The History Refresh Hour • Chapter 1 — What civic literacy looks like for adults • Chapter 2 — Reading a primary • Chapter 3 — Feed vs primary • Chapter 4 — Two accounts and corroboration • Chapter 5 — Civic texts as documents • Chapter 6 — Context, maps, and timelines on the go • Chapter 7 — Talking and writing a short civic claim • Chapter 8 — Keeping track • Chapter 9 — Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome This book exists because usable civic literacy is ordinary adult work — a feed card about a founding anniversary, a ballot pamphlet in the mail, a museum caption, a…
items.text: History Refresh for Adults Michael Gannotti 1 Figure 1: Cover History Refresh for Adults Michael Gannotti This illustrated edition is the teaching-manual of 13 September 2026. Endnotes run in one series. Chapter-opening images are original still-lifes, not portraits of persons or children. Documents still constrain the facts. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The History Refresh Hour • Chapter 1 — What civic literacy looks like for adults • Chapter 2 — Reading a primary • Chapter 3 — Feed vs primary • Chapter 4 — Two accounts and corroboration • Chapter 5 — Civic texts as documents • Chapter 6 — Context, maps, and timelines on the go • Chapter 7 — Talking and writing a short civic claim • Chapter 8 — Keeping track • Chapter 9 — Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome This book exists because usable civic literacy is ordinary adult work — a feed card about a founding anniversary, a ballot pamphlet in the mail, a museum caption, a courthouse plaque, a historic newspaper page, a short civic excerpt with a credit line, a workplace claim that “the law has always said.” There is you, the piece in front of you, and today’s looking move. You already have a life. The hour is the work. I wrote this for a capable, busy, willing adult. You may be on a train, at a desk, on a shift, in a trade bay, a clinic, a warehouse, a retail counter, or at a kitchen table after the kids are in bed. Many adults feel rusty when they sit down to history they last saw in school. That feeling is common. It is not a verdict, and it is not proof of a history gene. This book will make you fluent enough in today’s looking move to hear a caption offered as the event, a summary before a byline, a tidy “they were just stupid,” one account treated as a verdict, a model précis offered as a primary, and a feed-first reflex — and to ask yourself one good question before you grab the feed or the chatbot. You do not need to be a historian. You do need to hear a caption offered as the event, and to open the piece first. Ordinary stakes live on the go and in deeper sits: a pamphlet you already hold, a plaque, a museum label, a public-domain founding phrase, two short accounts of one event, a feed card about a clause. Civic life and work motivate. They do not replace the looking move. The cover says History Refresh for Adults. The work is this commute, this desk, this weekend sit. A job and a degree are not a bicycle you now ride on every document and every feed.1 You already consume history in pockets of life. That 1 Willingham, “Critical Thinking” (American Educator, 2007): thinking is not a bicycle skill. 4 WELCOME 5 is not the same as having rebuilt usable looking — primary before feed; source before body; a short claim with a named source and a named limit. Adulthood is not a civic birthday. A large adult skills survey places U.S. literacy near the international average — mean 258 versus about 260 — with about twenty-eight in a hundred U.S. adults at Level 1 or below.2 That survey is why dense founding prose needs short excerpts. It is not a grade for you. Named civic-fact surveys tell a limited story: many adults can name the three branches; fewer can name a Senate term.3 Those figures are population context, not this book’s pretest, and not historical thinking. The pamphlet or credited excerpt on the table tomorrow is the work. What a good History Refresh Hour looks like You sit down already knowing today’s looking move. An object is on the table — a short credited excerpt, a pamphlet page, a plaque photo, a historic newspaper header, a feed card you will treat as a later telling. You retrieve a little. Then you source before the body. Then you look — Observe, then Reflect, then Question — or you hop once off a feed to ask who is behind it. Then you try a parallel item unaided. Then you ask one good self-question and wait before the key, the feed, or the chatbot. Then you leave a short sticky or dated line you could almost show a colleague. The History Refresh Hour will teach this in full — micro-session, desk sit, weekend deep sit, talk-to-yourself shape, on-the-go and deeper try-its, and the AI rules once for adults. Later chapters will not reinvent it. Adults can rebuild usable civic literacy. Place by looking-move strip, not by birthA job and a diploma are domains — not all document and feed surfaces. Access date for URLs in these notes: 13 September 2026. 2 NCES/IES, Highlights from PIAAC 2023 (ages 16–65): U.S. literacy mean 258 vs international about 260; Level 1 or below 28% (was 19% in 2017; 2017 mean 271). Survey, not a trial of this book. Adjacent reading stock, not historical thinking. Not teen NAEP. Not mashed with PIAAC numeracy. 3 Annenberg Public Policy Center, Constitution Day Civics Survey 2025: 70% of U.S. adults named all three branches (was 65% in 2024); 79% named speech among First Amendment rights; 40% named a majority of First Amendment rights. Phone-to-internet methodology shift in 2023 — recent figures are not directly comparable to older phone eras. Pew Research Center short-read, 7 November 2023 (ATP, 5–11 June 2023, n=5,115): Court tenure about 75%; House apportionment 68%; chamber control about 66% / 63%; Senate term 44%; Electoral College tie 40%. Labelled population context. Not this book’s pretest. WELCOME 6 day and not by diploma year.4 A person who can name three branches is recalling. They have not finished the dual job of opening a piece before a thread and writing a short claim that names a source and a limit. We practice on surfaces you already meet. If you used History for Little Thinkers, History for Young Minds, History for Emerging Adults, or History for Homeschooling at a kitchen table, one pointer each, then this desk and this commute. Those books keep a parent in the room or a grade-by-grade survey. This book does not. You are the learner. This is not a reprint of those lesson banks. Publius owns the Federalist newspaper war at book length. One pointer for a Federalist deep week — then stay here. Critical Thinking for Adults owns presenttense reasons and myside craft. One pointer, then history. Math Refresher for Adults owns the commute/desk/weekend architecture and the rust rule. Literacy is not numeracy. One pointer, then history. What you will actually get Each teaching chapter does seven jobs, always in the same order. You will learn why this week’s looking move is worth the struggle, and understand it yourself. You will get a session you can run this week: named try-its across commute/lunch, desk-or-shift, and weekend deep sit, and a talk-to-yourself box. Tools stay optional. “Done enough” places by skill, not age or diploma year. The seven teaching chapters follow the looking-move strip, not twelve thin survey labels: what civic literacy looks like for adults (primary before feed); reading a primary; feed versus primary; two accounts and corroboration; civic texts as documents; context, maps, and timelines on the go; talking and writing a short civic claim. Keeping track and resources come last. Today you can put a pamphlet, a plaque, a credited excerpt, or a feed card on the table, name who made it and whether you are looking at the piece or at a feed about the piece, try a parallel item, and leave one exit sticky. 4 National Mathematics Advisory Panel, Foundations for Success (2008), Finding 15 — adult flip, continuity from Math Refresher for Adults: place by skill strip, not “too old.” Diploma year is not current looking skill. WELCOME 7 What this book will not do This book will not hand you 180 days of worksheets. Coverage is a map. Depth is the hour.5 It will not treat rust as destiny, a feed summary as the source, or naming three branches as graduation. It will not use teen test percentages as if they measured working adults. It will not invent History Refresh for Adults I, Emerging Adults History I, or a certificate of civic literacy. The promise is a path through ordinary civic life — not a fake diploma. It is not a reprint of the school-age history manuals named above, and it is not a sequel to Critical Thinking for Adults or Math Refresher for Adults. It is not a curriculum sales pitch or a guaranteed score. It is not a culture-war pamphlet, a campaign speech, or a Federalist monograph. It is not a weekly AP document dump. It is not medical advice, lending advice, or campaign speech dressed as civic literacy. We practice leaving a pamphlet, a plaque, a museum label, and a short credited civic excerpt. Live controversy stays off this table. The promise If you only remember one sentence, remember this: a path through ordinary adult civic life is the promise. A fake certificate is not. items.text: Math for Emerging Adults Michael Gannotti 1 Figure 1: Cover Math for Emerging Adults Michael Gannotti This illustrated edition is the teaching-manual of 5 September 2026. Endnotes run in one series. Chapter-opening images are original still-lifes, not portraits of persons or children. Documents still constrain the facts. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The Math Hour • Chapter 1 — Algebra I • Chapter 2 — Geometry with reasons • Chapter 3 — Algebra II • Chapter 4 — Precalculus and trigonometry • Chapter 5 — Calculus with meaning • Chapter 6 — Statistics and inference talk • Chapter 7 — Records • Chapter 8 — Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome This book exists because the math hour at your table is the whole program. There is no math department down the hall and no specialist waiting after lunch. There is you, a fifteen- to eighteen-year-old, and today’s idea — a solved equation with structure, a short proof with reasons, a function family read from a table, a unitcircle location, a rate that becomes instantaneous, or a sample number that is not yet a population claim. That is enough, if you know what to do with the hour. I wrote this for a capable, busy, willing parent of a fifteen- to eighteen-year-old. You may be teaching two ages at once, fifteen-to-sixteen and seventeen-toeighteen, at one table. You may be fitting a math sit between a job, a younger sibling, and a store run. You may love algebra, or you may remember high-school math as a fog of worksheets and a birthday that somehow meant Calculus. Many adults feel rusty when they sit down to teach high-school math they last saw as a student. That feeling is common. It is not a verdict. We will move on from it. This book will make you fluent enough in today’s idea to hear a wrong turn, and to ask a good question — without taking the pencil. You do not need to be a mathematician. You do need to hear letter-moving with no structure as a missing-meaning move, not a cute slip. You need to hear formulasheet geometry with no reason, “move and flip” as magic, quadratic formula before a graph or table, a regression button offered as family ID, SOHCAHTOA as the whole of trig, power-rule week with no rate story, a sample mean offered as a population claim, and a birthday offered as Calculus readiness. You need a session shape you can run on a Tuesday. You need a few sentences that actually help. That is the job. A path through ordinary high-school challenges — Algebra I with linear and quadratic meaning; geometry with reasons; Algebra II function families; precalculus and trig with the unit circle; calculus with rate, accumulation, and the Fundamental Theorem for ready students; statistics and inference talk — is possi4 WELCOME 5 ble at a kitchen table. The path is not a personality trait and it is not a percentile. It is a small set of moves, practiced with you in the chair. About 3.4 percent of U.S. students ages 5–17 were homeschooled in 2022–23 — roughly 1.765 million children.1 In the high-school grades, ages that map to grades 9–12, the cell is about 3.1 percent.2 That figure is context, not a ranking. Many readers of this book will not be in that pond. They will be after-school, weekend, or kitchen-table parents of enrolled adolescents. The moves still fit. Homeschooling is legal in all fifty states and the District of Columbia. The paperwork is not one load: Texas asks almost nothing of the state agency; New York asks for a written plan and regular reports.3 There is no national homeschool diploma and no national “Emerging Adults Math I” credit.4 Math is the usual required or assumed high-school object.5 In the last federal tables that listed subjects taught at home, 1 Ellena Sempeles and Jiashan Cui, Parent and Family Involvement in Education: 2023, NCES 2024-113 (Washington, DC: National Center for Education Statistics, September 2024), Table A-6: 3.4 percent homeschooled, approximately 1,765,000 students, ages 5–17 with a K–12 grade equivalent, 2022–23; grades 9–12 cell 3.1 percent. https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2024/2024113.pdf. Access date for URLs in these notes: 5 September 2026. Latest federal count this book uses; not a 2026 national total. A neighboring 5.2 percent received instruction at home (homeschooled or full-time virtual) and is a different bucket. 2 Ellena Sempeles and Jiashan Cui, Parent and Family Involvement in Education: 2023, NCES 2024-113 (Washington, DC: National Center for Education Statistics, September 2024), Table A-6: 3.4 percent homeschooled, approximately 1,765,000 students, ages 5–17 with a K–12 grade equivalent, 2022–23; grades 9–12 cell 3.1 percent. https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2024/2024113.pdf. Access date for URLs in these notes: 5 September 2026. Latest federal count this book uses; not a 2026 national total. A neighboring 5.2 percent received instruction at home (homeschooled or full-time virtual) and is a different bucket. 3 Texas Education Agency, “Home Schooling,” https://tea.texas.gov/families-andstudents/finding-school-your-child/home-schooling. New York State Education Department, “Home Instruction Questions and Answers,” https://www.nysed.gov/nonpublic-schools/homeinstruction-questions-and-answers. Homeschooling is legal in all fifty states and D.C.; these two pages illustrate a light-process and a heavier-process pattern, not a national template. This book is not legal advice. 4 Texas Education Agency, “Home Schooling”: the State of Texas does not award a diploma to students that are home schooled. New York State Education Department, “Home Instruction Questions and Answers”: a high school diploma may only be awarded to a student enrolled in a registered secondary school. North Carolina Division of Non-Public Education, “Home School Records Retention & Diplomas FAQs,” https://www.doa.nc.gov/divisions/non-publiceducation/home-schools/faqs/records-retention-diplomas: the State does not issue a diploma or a transcript; the home-school chief administrator does. “Emerging Adults Math I” is not a credit in any opened statute. 5 Texas Education Agency, “Alternative Schooling,” restating Leeper: bona fide instruction us- WELCOME 6 the high-school math rows for grades 9–12 that year were Algebra I at 33 percent, Algebra II at 33 percent, Geometry at 26 percent, Calculus at 13 percent — and arithmetic still at 31 percent.6 The hour in front of you is the work. Placement into Algebra I, Geometry, Algebra II, Precalculus, Calculus, or Statistics is by skill, not by birthday. This book is not a reprint. Math for Young Minds is for ages 11–14. One pointer, if you have a younger sibling at the table. Then we teach at fifteen to eighteen. Math for Little Thinkers is for ages 5–10. One pointer, if you need the early years. Then we teach here. Mathematics for Homeschooling covers grades 1–12. It compressed high school into survey chapters. One pointer, if you need the whole-span map. Then we teach here. This book is not a sequel. Critical Thinking for Emerging Adults is the same house, a different subject and a different age band — Arnett’s 18–25 is not this band. One pointer, then we teach this age’s math. Two refusals belong on the first day. Birthday is not Calculus readiness. An eighteen-year-old missing linear and quadratic structure does Algebra I repair without apology; a fifteen-year-old ready for limits may begin calculus meaning with supervision — skill and motivation, not a race.7 Letter-moving and formula-sheet geometry are not high-school mathematics with meaning. Structure, reasons, and ing a written curriculum that includes math. North Carolina Division of Non-Public Education: annual nationally standardized test including mathematics. Pennsylvania 24 P.S. § 13-1327.1: elementary and secondary subject lists include arithmetic or mathematics. Virginia Department of Education, “Home Instruction”: the parent writes a list of subjects. New York 8 NYCRR 100.10: required subjects by grade band include arithmetic or mathematics. None of these five opened maps names a critical-thinking course. Math is the usual required or assumed high-school object. The parent reads their own statute. 6 Jiashan Cui and Rachel Hanson, Homeschooling in the United States: Results from the 2012 and 2016 Parent and Family Involvement Survey, NCES 2020-001 (Washington, DC: National Center for Education Statistics, 2019), Table 9: among grades 9–12 homeschoolers that year, Algebra I taught 33 percent; Algebra II taught 33 percent; Geometry taught 26 percent; Calculus taught 13 percent; arithmetic still taught 31 percent. Quote the high-school math rows. Do not reuse the elementary arithmetic 83/86 cells or the middle 66/41 cells as this band. The 2023 First Look did not republish the subject-taught tables. https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2020/2020001.pdf. 7 National Mathematics Advisory Panel, Foundations for Success: The Final Report of the National Mathematics Advisory Panel (Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, 2008), Critical Foundations of Algebra: proficiency with whole numbers, fractions (including decimals and percents), and certain aspects of geometry and measurement — continuity if unfinished. Finding 10: conceptual understanding, computational fluency, and problem-solving skills belong together. Finding 15: claims that children of particular ages cannot learn certain content because they are “too young,” “not in the appropriate stage,” or “not ready” have consistently been shown to be wrong if prerequisite knowledge is present. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED500695.pdf. WELCOME 7 representations come before the shortcut. What a good math hour looks like You sit down already knowing today’s idea. An object is on the table — a solved problem on scrap paper, a marked geometry diagram, function-family table cards, a unit circle, a rate or accumulation sketch, sample-versus-population sticky notes. The student warms up on facts they can already get right. You model one solved problem out loud, short — graph or table visible beside the algebra. Then they try, and you wait. You ask one good question — not “did you get it?” but “If this is linear, what stays constant — the rate or the second difference?” or “What are we given? What must we show? What bridge gets us there?” Three seconds feels long. It is the work. Practice mixes the new move with last week’s. The hour ends with one or two items they do alone. You stop talking sooner than feels polite. The student talks and builds. You hold the key. That is the hour. Forty-five to seventyfive minutes is the usual ambition; ninety when a proof or a calculus investigation needs it. The next long piece of this front matter, The Math Hour, will teach it in full. Later chapters will not reinvent it. WELCOME 8 Figure 2: A kitchen-table math hour with a solved problem and a marked diagram Students this age already do high-school mathematics. They do not become Calculus-ready because a candle was lit, and they do not become algebra-fluent because they can chant “move and flip.” What you will actually get Each teaching chapter does eight jobs, always in the same order, so you are never hunting for the move. You will learn why this week’s idea is worth the struggle. You will understand it yourself, with the wrong answers you should be able to hear. You will get a session you can run this week: exact wording, named try-its in and out of the home, and a talk box. Your student will get a short section of their own. If it isn’t clicking, three diagnostics and a next move. Tools, including AI, stay optional and adult- WELCOME 9 side. And you will get a plain checklist for “done enough,” so you can place by skill rather than by birthday. The six teaching chapters follow the work: Algebra I; geometry with reasons; Algebra II function families; precalculus and trigonometry; calculus with meaning for ready students; statistics and inference talk. Records and resources come last. Calculus is for the ready — not ever…

There is no math department down the hall and no specialist waiting after lunch. There is you, an eleven- to fourteen-year-old, and today’s idea — a ratio table or a number line that runs both ways, a question worth waiting for, an equation they write and check. That is enough, if you know what to do with the hour. I wrote this for a capable, busy, willing parent of an eleven- to fourteen-year-old. You may be teaching two ages at once, eleven-to-twelve and thirteen-to-fourteen, at one table. You may be fitting a math sit between a job, a younger sibling, and a store run. You may love number, or you may remember middle-grades math as a fog of worksheets and a birthday that somehow meant Algebra I. Many adults feel rusty when they sit down to teach. That feeling is common. It is not a verdict. We will move on from it. This book will make you fluent enough in today’s idea to hear a wrong turn, and to ask a good question — without taking the pencil. You do not need to be a mathematician. You do need to hear cross-multiply with no ratio table as a missing-meaning move, not a cute slip. You need to hear “of means multiply,” = as “write the answer,” pizza offered as the number −3/4, lettermoving without structure, a formula card offered as geometry, and a birthday offered as Algebra I readiness. You need a session shape you can run on a Tuesday. You need a few sentences that actually help. That is the job. A path through ordinary middle-grades challenges — fractions, decimals, and percents as numbers (including negatives), ratio and proportion with meaning, signed numbers, expressions, equations by same-to-both-sides, early functions and linear thinking, geometry with reasons, data and chance with story-problem schemas — is possible at a kitchen table. The path is not a personality trait and it is not a percentile. It is a small set of moves, practiced on mathematics the student already somewhat knows, with you in the chair. 4 WELCOME 5 About 3.4 percent of U.S. students ages 5–17 were homeschooled in 2022–23 — roughly 1.765 million children.1 In the middle grades, ages that map to grades 6–8, the cell is about 3.0 percent.2 That figure is context, not a ranking. You are one of those tables. Many readers of this book will not be in that pond. They will be afterschool, weekend, or kitchen-table parents of enrolled adolescents. The moves still fit. Homeschooling is legal in all fifty states and the District of Columbia. The paperwork is not one load: Texas asks almost nothing of the state agency; New York asks for a written plan and regular reports.3 There is no national homeschool diploma and no national “Young Minds Math I” credit.4 None of Texas, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Virginia, or New York requires a critical-thinking course. items.summary: Usable mathematics is ordinary adult work: a number on a line, a unit price on a shelf, a percent on a dashboard, a short reason for a measurement. A working adult who is not a mathematician can run that hour on a train, at a desk, on a shift — if “of means multiply” is heard as a keyword grab, not a schema, and a calculator output is not allowed to pass as sense.

items.text: Math Refresher for Adults Michael Gannotti 1 Figure 1: Cover Math Refresher for Adults Michael Gannotti This illustrated edition is the teaching-manual of 5 September 2026. Endnotes run in one series. Chapter-opening images are original still-lifes, not portraits of persons or children. Documents still constrain the facts. 2 Contents • Welcome • How to Use This Book This Week • If You Only Remember Five Things • The Refresh Hour • Chapter 1 — Number sense, fractions, and decimals as numbers • Chapter 2 — Percent and ratio • Chapter 3 — Algebra refresh • Chapter 4 — Geometry with reasons • Chapter 5 — Functions and trigonometry • Chapter 6 — Calculus edges • Chapter 7 — Statistics for life and work • Chapter 8 — Keeping track • Chapter 9 — Resources • A Note on Sources 3 Welcome This book exists because usable mathematics is ordinary adult work — a number on a line, a base on a paycheck, a unit price on a shelf, a percent on a dashboard, a short reason for a measurement, a rate in units, a sample labelled as a sample. There is you, the object in front of you, and today’s idea. You already have a life. The hour is the work. I wrote this for a capable, busy, willing adult. You may be on a train, at a desk, on a shift, in a trade bay, a clinic, a warehouse, a retail counter, or at a kitchen counter before work. Many adults feel rusty when they sit down to math they last saw in school. That feeling is common. It is not a verdict, and it is not proof of a math gene.1 This book will make you fluent enough in today’s idea to hear a keyword percent that is not yet a schema, letter-moving with no structure, a formula with no reason, a sample mean offered as a population claim, a calculator output offered as sense, and a photo-to-key offered as practice — and to ask yourself one good question before you grab the answer. You do not need to be a mathematician. You do need to hear “of means multiply” as a keyword grab, not a schema. Ordinary stakes live on the go and in deeper sits: a paycheck stub, an APR disclosure row (structure, not product advice), a unit-price tag, a cooking scale, a map scale, a DIY cut list, a sports box-score rate, a dashboard percent, a pharmacy label rate (units and rate only — not medical advice).2 Money, health leaflets, cars, and work decks motivate. They do not replace the balanced equation, the ratio that means, or the rate meaning. 1 Maloney and Beilock; Beilock and Willingham on math anxiety: loads working memory; “not a numbers person” language is real. Not a clinical protocol in this book. Access date for URLs in these notes: 5 September 2026. 2 CFPB: interest rate and APR are not the same; compare APR to APR. Pharmacy try-its use rate and units only — not dosing advice. 4 WELCOME 5 The cover says Math Refresher for Adults. The work is this commute, this desk, this weekend sit. A job, a degree, and years of experience are not a bicycle you now ride on every quantitative surface.3 You already compute in pockets of life and work. That is not the same as having rebuilt meaning and fluency across the skill strips this book teaches. Adulthood is not a math birthday. A large adult skills survey places U.S. numeracy below the international average — mean 249 versus 263 — with about one in three U.S. adults at Level 1 or below.4 That survey is context for why a refresher exists. It is not a grade for you, and it is not a finding that this book raises a score. The stub, the shelf tag, or the number line on the table tomorrow is the work. What a good refresh hour looks like You sit down already knowing today’s idea. An object is on the table — a stub, a shelf tag, a number-line scrap, a solved problem, a marked diagram, a dashboard tile, a recipe card. You retrieve a little. Then you talk yourself through a solved example. Then you try a parallel item unaided. Then you ask one good self-question and wait before the key. Then you leave a short sticky or dated line you could almost show a colleague. The Refresh Hour will teach this in full — micro-session, desk sit, weekend deep sit, talk-to-yourself shape, on-the-go and deeper try-its, and the AI rules once for adults. Later chapters will not reinvent it. 3 Willingham, “Critical Thinking” (American Educator, 2007): thinking is not a bicycle skill. A job and a diploma are domains — not all quantitative surfaces. 4 NCES/IES, Highlights from PIAAC 2023 (ages 16–65): U.S. numeracy mean 249 vs international 263; Level 1 or below 34% (was 29% in 2017). Survey, not a trial of this book. Not teen NAEP. WELCOME 6 Figure 2: A refresh-hour setup Adults can rebuild usable mathematics with meaning. Place by skill strip, not by birthday and not by diploma year.5 Conceptual understanding, computational fluency, and problem solving belong together.6 A person who can tip a bill in their head is computing. They have not finished the dual job of hearing a wrong turn and trying a parallel item before a tool finishes the attempt. We practice on surfaces you already meet. If you used Math for Little Thinkers, Math for Young Minds, Math for Emerging Adults, or Mathematics for Homeschooling at a kitchen table, one pointer each, then this desk and this commute. Those books keep a parent in the room and a student section on the page. This book does not. You are the learner. The 5 National Mathematics Advisory Panel, Foundations for Success (2008), Finding 15: place by skill strip, not “too old.” Finding 4 / Critical Foundations still gate algebra. 6 NMAP Finding 10: conceptual understanding, computational fluency, and problem solving belong together. WELCOME 7 seven headings still work. Content names overlap in places — algebra, geometry, functions, calculus edges, stats. Audience and pedagogy do not. This is not a reprint of those lesson banks. There is you, the object in front of you, and today’s idea. You already have a life. The hour is the work. I wrote this for a capable, busy, willing adult. You may be on a train, at a desk, on a shift, in a trade bay, a clinic, a warehouse, a retail counter, or at a kitchen counter before work. Many adults feel rusty when they sit down to math they last saw in school. That feeling is common. It is not a verdict, and it is not proof of a math gene.1 This book will make you fluent enough in today’s idea to hear a keyword percent that is not yet a schema, letter-moving with no structure, a formula with no reason, a sample mean offered as a population claim, a calculator output offered as sense, and a photo-to-key offered as practice — and to ask yourself one good question before you grab the answer. You do not need to be a mathematician. You do need to hear “of means multiply” as a keyword grab, not a schema. Ordinary stakes live on the go and in deeper sits: a paycheck stub, an APR disclosure row (structure, not product advice), a unit-price tag, a cooking scale, a map scale, a DIY cut list, a sports box-score rate, a dashboard percent, a pharmacy label rate (units and rate only — not medical advice).2 Money, health leaflets, cars, and work decks motivate. Documents do the work. The popular story does not survive.
