items.text: Francis of Assisi: An Unpossessed Life WisdomForge Booklet — Adult Francis of Assisi: An Unpossessed Life WisdomForge Booklet — Adult ——— About This Book Adults do not need another birdbath. They need a man who made money nervous, made war look theologically illiterate, and then told his own brothers not to explain him into something they could fund. Francis of Assisi (1181/82–1226) left a short corpus. Treat it as a veto. Armstrong and Brady’s Francis and Clare: The Complete Works is the English door. Thomas of Celano (1228) is early official memory. Augustine Thompson (2012) is the biography that will not let you rest in a fresco. John Tolan (2009) will show you your own century hiding in Damietta. David Burr and Malcolm Lambert will not let poverty stay a mood. This band is for rooms you actually inhabit: a parish finance meeting, a family inheritance, a hospital corridor, a climate board, an interfaith dinner, a hiring conversation about “culture fit.” Practice items are protocols with deliverables. They are not pastoral care and not medical advice. Six chapters, same spine as the younger bands, different job: you get the fights, the documents, and the places where reception becomes recruitment. ——— Chapter 1: The Palate, Not the Brand Illustration for Chapter 1 Francis’s own origin story is not a brand deck. It is a change in taste. “The Lord gave me, Brother Francis, thus to begin doing penance in this way: for when I was in sin, it seemed too bitter a thing to see lepers. And the Lord Himself led me among them and I showed mercy to them. And when I departed from them, what had seemed bitter to me was changed into sweetness of soul and body. And afterwards I delayed a little and left the world.” — *Testament* (1226) Adults love origin stories that can be scheduled. This one cannot. The Lord leads. Mercy is shown. The body — not only the opinions — flips from bitter to sweet. Then delay. Then leaving. If your conversion narrative has no delay, you may be narrating a rebrand. Medieval leprosy was a social death: walls, bells, dissolved rights, a theology of visible curse (Demaitre; the civil/canon practices Thompson assumes). Coming close is not “volunteering.” It is crossing a purity regime. Wolf’s question — did Francis need the leper more than the leper needed Francis? — belongs in an adult room because adults know how to use other people’s pain as spiritual capital. The Testament does not do a victory lap. That is evidence. It is not an acquittal. The leper still becomes an origin forever. Hold both. Collestrada and the Perugia prison (1202–3) emptied knighthood. They did not teach him whom to touch. Assisi’s minores had already won a commune fight in 1198. He is not a peasant with no other move. He is a winner’s son leaving the win. Pietro cannot parse that as charity because charity, in a shop, leaves the shop standing. Celano will offer a speaking crucifix at San Damiano. Francis’s last will does not. Adult reading privileges the will for beginnings. You may still love the crucifix scene. You may not let it overrule the document the dying man chose. Scholarly debate, at adult length: ethical conversion versus mystical conversion is a false fork here. The text is mystical because it is carnal — sweetness of soul and body. A seminar that cannot hear “the Lord led me” will sociologize him into a case. A parish that cannot hear Wolf will saint him into a user of the poor. Neither room is honest alone. Hagiography is five jobs, not one book. Layer 1 is Francis’s own corpus — Canticle, Testament, Rules, letters, prayers — a veto, not a memoir. Layer 2 is Celano’s Vita Prima (1228–29), commissioned after canonization, already selecting for a saint, then Vita Secunda (1247) to correct and thicken from further testimony. Layer 3 is Bonaventure’s Legenda Maior (1263): a Minister General’s unification, an alter Christus coherent enough to hold an order already splitting over poverty, and the sidelining of messier earlier lives. Layer 4 is the Fioretti, late fourteenth century, more than a hundred years out: wolf, birds, crib as folk devotion. Layer 5 is Thompson and the Early Documents project, which treat the layers as evidence rather than as a single fresco. Conversion is the test case. Celano needs a speaking crucifix and a kiss. Francis, dying, names a leper and a delay. Letting Layer 2 overrule Layer 1 is not “richer.” It is a different beginning. Conservative readers inside the tradition hold that early narrative cores are sound even when miracles are later paint. Critical readers strip hagiographic jobs to recover a reformer who is more human and less miraculous. Hermeneutic readers refuse the strip: how Francis was perceived is part of what he historically became. You need all three methods. None of them gets to invent a saying. The Testament’s “the Lord gave me” formula — conversion, churches, brothers, Gospel form, priests, peace greeting — is Matura’s received vocation, not a personal brand. Adults who have rewritten their origin stories for a hiring packet should hear the difference. Received is not passive. He walks, strips, sails, hides wounds. Received is the opposite of sovereign. Collestrada and Perugia emptied knighthood of glamour. They did not teach him whom to touch. Assisi’s minores had already won in 1198. He is a winner’s son leaving the win. Pietro cannot parse that as charity because charity, in a shop, leaves the shop standing. Social death (Demaitre; civil and canon practice) means the leprosaria sit outside walls for a reason: property, marriage, church access, a theology of visible curse. Coming close is not volunteering. It is crossing a purity regime. Wolf’s question — did Francis need the leper more than the leper needed Francis? — belongs at an adult table because adults know how to use other people’s pain as spiritual capital. The Testament does not do a victory lap. That is evidence. It is not an acquittal. The leper still becomes an origin forever. Hold both, or you will get a tract. The founding sentence belongs beside the leper, because the same grammar of gift structures both: “And after the Lord gave me some brothers, no one showed me what I should do, but the Most High Himself revealed to me that I should live according to the form of the Holy Gospel. And I had this written down simply and in few words, and the Lord Pope confirmed it for me.” — *Testament* Three agents: Most High, Francis as scribe of few words, pope as confirmer. Remove any one and you get a different movement: pure interiority, founder-cult, or curia. Adults who have founded a nonprofit, a parish ministry, or a company will recognize the triangle and how it stops being equilateral. Delay is still doctrine. The brothers arrive after the leper, not instead of the leper. A room that wants a scalable origin without a socially dead body is already glossing. Hospital corridors make this expensive. You already have a protocol below. The point of putting it after the triangle is not to turn Francis into a chaplaincy manual. It is to notice that your nervous system still has a bell — the signal that says “approach carefully” — and that Francis named the bell as the beginning of theology. Wolf remains in the room: using the corridor as your turning-point story, without the people in it getting a life after your turning, is spiritual capital. The Testament does not acquit you. It only refuses a conversion that never had to come close. Adults love origin stories that can be scheduled. This one cannot. If your conversion narrative has no delay, you may be narrating a rebrand. A hiring packet that turns a leper into a “formative experience” without remainder is Wolf’s question in a suit. Privilege the will for beginnings even when you love Celano’s crucifix. You may not let a set piece overrule the document the dying man chose. The first Franciscan theology is proximity to the socially dead, received as gift, undergone as a change in the nervous system. Delay is part of the doctrine. So is the body. Dualism loses. So does a purely sociological reduction that cannot hear “the Lord led me.” Neither a seminar nor a parish is honest alone. Big Idea The first Franciscan theology is proximity to the socially dead, received as gift, undergone as a change in the nervous system. Delay is part of the doctrine. Practice 1. Hospital / care-home corridor (no advice, a protocol). With permission of whoever holds the door, sit for twenty minutes where you usually pass. Afterward, write 400 words on what your body did — recoil, hurry, joke, phone. Do not write a moral. Deliverable: the 400 words, unread by the people you watched. 2. Inheritance table. At the next family money conversation, notice who is treated as already dead to the decision. One page to yourself after. No sending it to the group chat. 3. Read-aloud. Read the Testament leper paragraph aloud to one other adult. Ask them what verb they do not believe. Write their verb down. 4. Thompson, one chapter on the conversion years. List two places he will not follow Celano. Deliverable: two citations. Reflect Whom have you used as a turning point in your story, and did they get a life after your turning? ——— Chapter 2: Coin as a Spiritual Technology Illustration for Chapter 2 Lady Poverty is courtly love aimed at the thing a merchant’s town exists to flee. Adults should hear the class: Pietro’s wealth is coin, credit, cloth — the new measure — not only land. “And let the brothers not appropriate anything to themselves, neither house nor place nor anything. And as pilgrims and strangers in this world, serving the Lord in poverty and humility, let them go with confidence to seek alms.” — Later Rule, ch. 6 Pilgrim and stranger are not aesthetics. They are a legal mood: you do not file a deed on the inn. “Spiritual friends” who hold the coin you will not touch are the adult problem in seed. You have sat on boards that keep the mission sentence and move the money offstage. You know the elegance. You know the leak. Later Rule 4 writes the nerve and then the valve: “I strictly command all my brothers not to receive coins or money in any form, either personally or through intermediaries. Nevertheless, the ministers and custodians alone may take special care through their spiritual friends to provide for the needs of the sick and the clothing of the others according to places, seasons and cold climates, as they judge necessary, saving always that, as stated above, they do not receive coins or money.” — Later Rule, ch. 4 The first sentence is absolute. The second keeps it and routes coin through friends and officers. Spirituals will call the route a fiction. Conventuals will call it how a hospital gets blankets. Francis is already inside the contradiction while alive. Chapter 5 then refuses idle holiness: “Those brothers to whom the Lord has given the grace of working may work faithfully and devotedly so that, while avoiding idleness, the enemy of the soul, they do not extinguish the Spirit of holy prayer and devotion to which all temporal things must contribute. In payment for their work they may receive whatever is necessary for the bodily support of themselves and their brothers, excepting coin or money, and let them do this humbly as is becoming for servants of God and followers of most holy poverty.” — Later Rule, ch. 5 Pay as food and cloth, not as coin. Prayer as the thing work must not kill. That is a different economy from a wage as proof of worth and a different economy from a professional beggar with a holy face. “And I worked with my hands, and I still desire to work; and I firmly wish that all my brothers give themselves to honest work. … And when we are not paid for our work, let us have recourse to the Lord’s table, begging alms from door to door.” — *Testament* Idle holiness and hoarding craft are both refused. Adult economies make wage the proof of worth. Francis will not. He also will not bless a professional beggar with a…

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Triangle — Most High, Few
chapters.text: Words, Pope Illustration for Chapter 3 San Damiano’s voice is Celano. Francis’s churches are a prayer: “We adore You, Lord Jesus Christ, here and in all Your churches throughout the whole world, and we bless You, because by Your holy cross You have redeemed the world.” — *Testament* And the early petition: “Most High, glorious God, enlighten the darkness of my heart and give me true faith, certain hope, and perfect charity, sense and knowledge, Lord, so that I may carry out Your holy and true command.” — Prayer before the Crucifix Adults who have left churches because buildings disappointed them should sit with “all Your churches.” Repair is intramural. The Eucharist sentence, from the Testament, makes the dropout myth expensive: “I see nothing corporally in this world of the Son of God except His most holy Body and Blood, which they receive and which they alone administer to others.” — *Testament* The Letter to the Entire Order is a second witness, not a restatement. Dying, he kisses their feet on paper and aims them at the altar: “Wherefore, brothers, kissing your feet and with the charity of which I am capable, I conjure you all to show all reverence and all honor possible to the most holy Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom the things that are in heaven and the things that are on earth are pacified and reconciled to Almighty God.” — *Letter to the Entire Order* He is a deacon. He does not found a parallel altar. He also does not let clergy become décor. The proto-Protestant reading fails here in public, not only in a Grown-Up appendix. Francis submitted to papal approval, revered the consecrated host as real presence, accepted confession and priests, placed Portiuncula under Mary, and never challenged Catholic doctrine. He challenged clerical wealth, rigidity, lay exclusion, and distance from the poor. Those are reforms of practice from inside a Church he would not leave. Luther is not a delayed Francis. Francis is not an early Luther. Claiming him…

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: Chapter 4: Kinship After the Managerial Age
chapters.text: Illustration for Chapter 4 The Canticle’s grammar will not hire you as a steward-CEO of a dead warehouse. “Praised be You, my Lord, with all Your creatures, especially Sir Brother Sun, who is the day and through whom You give us light. And he is beautiful and radiant with great splendor; and bears a likeness of You, Most High One.” Through. Likeness. Not identity. The rest of the Canticle must be on the page, or the birdbath wins by excerpt: “Praised be You, my Lord, through Sister Moon and the stars; in heaven You formed them clear and precious and beautiful. Praised be You, my Lord, through Brother Wind, and through the air, cloudy and serene, and every kind of weather through which You give sustenance to Your creatures. Praised be You, my Lord, through Sister Water, which is very useful and humble and precious and chaste. Praised be You, my Lord, through Brother Fire, through whom You light the night; and he is beautiful and playful and robust and strong. Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Mother Earth, who sustains and governs us, and who produces various fruits with colored flowers and herbs.” — *Canticle of the Creatures* Sister Water is humble and chaste. Sister Mother Earth governs. Adults who sit on climate boards should feel the insult to managerial exceptionalism. Stewardship can still loot politely. Kinship makes looting a family crime. Weather includes cloudy days. Fire is playful and dangerous. The pantheist reading fails in public here, not only in a high-band appendix. If Brother Sun were God, Francis would not need likeness. Sacrament is not identity. The sun is vestige; Christ is image. Collapse those and you get idolatry dressed as ecology. Keep them without kinship and you get a warehouse. Nature is created, not divine. Praise runs through creatures, not as them. Sorrell tests whether “nature mystic” survives the preposition. Delio maps sacrament. White (1967) needed an exception to a Christian villain story. He did not need an honorary…

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Chapter 5: A Walk That Converted No One
chapters.text: Illustration for Chapter 5 Peace is not the unattributed poster. It is a revealed greeting. “And the Lord revealed to me that I should say the greeting, ‘The Lord give you peace,’ which I previously did not use.” — *Testament* Rank-flattening. John 20 in the street. Cheap if you let it be. “And if he should fall a thousand times, let him be received back.” — Letter to a Minister Adults who manage people know exile is efficient. Francis forbids efficiency as the first tool. He does not forbid truth. Reception is not amnesia. Early Rule 16: “And the brothers who go among the Saracens… can live among them spiritually… or, when they see it pleases God, announce the word of God.” Damietta 1219: Fifth Crusade, Pelagius, hunger, plunder-as-piety (Powell). Francis and Illuminatus cross. Beaten. Al-Kamil — cultured, Saladin’s nephew — listens, in Celano’s “great attention.” Gifts refused. No baptism. Safe return. Warning against attack, ignored. Later fire and secret conversion fail early sources (Tolan). Three readings, all partly true: missionary, encounter, prophetic protest. A medieval Catholic who thinks Islam false can still refuse a sword. Courtesy is not pluralism. Conversion is not courtesy. Keep the sentence in that double state. Letters to rulers: power is temporary; honor the Body; remember the poor. A camp that gambles under a cross is a liturgical crisis before it is a military one. The letter itself, not only its reputation: “To all podestàs, and consuls, judges and governors, in whatever part of the world, and to all others to whom this letter may come, Brother Francis, your little and contemptible servant, wishes health and peace to you. Consider and see that the day of death draws nigh. I ask you, therefore, with such reverence as I can, not to forget the Lord on account of the cares and solicitudes of this world and not to turn aside from His commandments… And when the day of death comes, all that which they think they have shall be taken away from them.…

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: Chapter 6: Gloves, Sister Death, and the
chapters.text: Treasury Illustration for Chapter 6 La Verna, September 1224. Celano’s seraph and marks; companions see; gloves; pain; first widely attested stigmatic. Dante’s “final seal” (Paradiso XI) is meaning, not a lab note. He will not write the spectacle. He writes the altar. Hiddenness fits a divine name: “You are holy, Lord God, the only God, who does wonderful things. You are strong. You are great. You are the Most High. You are love. You are wisdom. You are humility. You are patience.” — *Praises of God* (for Brother Leo) Display would be a different god. The only surviving autograph is not a wound-report: “Blessing and all good, the Lord give you. Brother Francis.” — Blessing of Brother Leo (autograph, c. 1224–1225) Master refused in ink. Esser on the autograph is the scholarly reminder: the one scrap in his hand chooses “Brother.” Mechanism stays open. The marks were real in the only sense a historian can use: early sources, companions, persistence. Thomas of Celano describes black marks and a side that often bled — more restrained than later art. Interpretation is theological: imitation becoming participation; seraph as burning love united to crucifixion. Medical options remain: psychosomatic Passion-attention (real bodily effects of intense religious experience, poorly studied), pre-existing disease (malaria, malnutrition, possible tuberculoid lesions consistent with known illness), miracle. Self-infliction is possible in theory and poorly matched to the sources. We do not have enough evidence to diagnose from eight centuries. Meaning does not wait on mechanism. Glibness — credulous or sneering — is the only forbidden affect. The stigmata introduced a new criterion of sanctity: bodily conformity during life, not only wonders at a tomb (Vauchez). After Francis, cases multiply; his is the archetype. Doubt is as old as the claim. This booklet will not close a courtroom. It will not pretend the question is unserious. “Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Bodily…

items.text: Francis of Assisi: Without Gloss WisdomForge Booklet — Ages 15–18 Francis of Assisi: Without Gloss WisdomForge Booklet — Ages 15–18 ——— About This Book You already know a Francis. He is usually wrong. The birdbath Francis is a Layer-4 folk saint. The “instrument of your peace” Francis is a twentieth-century poem wearing a brown habit. The dropout Francis who “just loved Jesus and hated the Church” collides with a deacon who would adore the Eucharist in every church he could crawl into. The ecological Francis is more defensible — the Canticle is his — but only if you keep the Most High in the first line. This booklet argues. It uses Francis’s own corpus (Armstrong and Brady, Francis and Clare: The Complete Works) as a veto over later lives. It uses Thomas of Celano (1228) as early, official, and already selective. It uses Augustine Thompson (2012) as a check on both. It will not resolve the stigmata in a lab. It will not pretend Damietta was an interfaith summit. It will not pretend poverty was a lifestyle brand. Six sittings: leper and the social dead; Lady Poverty and coin; Rule, gloss, and institution; creation as vestige not idol; Damietta’s “or”; La Verna, Sister Death, and the long civil war over his will. If you want a mascot, stop here. If you want a problem that still cuts, read on. ——— Chapter 1: The Social Dead and the First Theology Illustration for Chapter 1 You are trained to look for a conversion scene with weather: light, voice, collapse. Francis denies you that as the beginning. In the Testament, the first theology is a body he could not stand. “The Lord gave me, Brother Francis, thus to begin doing penance in this way: for when I was in sin, it seemed too bitter a thing to see lepers. And the Lord Himself led me among them and I showed mercy to them. And when I departed from them, what had seemed bitter to me was changed into sweetness of soul and body. And afterwards I delayed a little and left the world.” Four movements: bitterness, being led, mercy, sweetness. Then delay. Then leaving. The sequence wrecks two modern sermons. One sermon says insight precedes action. Francis acts, then the palate changes. The other sermon says conversion is instantaneous. He delays. The seed is dated; the plant is not a firework. Assisi’s leprosaria sat outside walls because medieval Christianity had fused illness with a purity code. Luke Demaitre’s medical history and the civil/canon practices of “social death” (property, marriage, church access) mean Francis is not performing a random kindness. He is crossing a legal and liturgical line. Touch is policy. Kenneth Baxter Wolf asked whether the leper is a stage for a merchant’s son’s drama. Take the objection at full strength. Hagiography loves the kiss on the road; Francis does not narrate the kiss. He narrates mercy and a sensory inversion. That is less cinematic and harder to dismiss as cosplay. Still, a last will that makes a leper the origin of a world-famous order does use that body forever. Ethical reading holds both: the encounter is real solidarity and it becomes capital in a saint’s archive. Collestrada (1202) and the Perugia prison are not the origin he chooses. They are conditions. Communal Italy taught him that walls change owners (imperial sack, 1174; commune revolt, 1198; papal orbit). A year with someone else’s keys can empty knighthood of glamour without teaching you whom to touch. The leper teaches whom to touch. Celano will later give you San Damiano’s speaking crucifix as a set piece. Francis’s Testament does not. For this chapter, let the silence govern. The historical Francis, if we privilege Layer 1, locates God first in the person the town had declared a curse. Hagiography is not one book. It is five jobs stacked on one man (Harry 7.2). Layer 1 is Francis’s own corpus: Canticle, Testament, Rules, letters, prayers — not a memoir, but a veto. Layer 2 is Thomas of Celano’s Vita Prima (1228–29), commissioned after canonization, already selecting for a saint, then Vita Secunda (1247) to correct and thicken. Layer 3 is Bonaventure’s Legenda Maior (1263): a Minister General’s unification, a coherent alter Christus, and the order to sideline messier earlier lives. Layer 4 is the Fioretti (late 14th century): wolf, birds, crib as folk devotion, more than a hundred years out. Layer 5 is Thompson and the Early Documents project, which treat the layers as evidence rather than as a single fresco. The closer you stand to Layer 1, the more anxious, sacramental, and uncute the man. The farther you stand, the more the garden statue wins. Conversion is the test case. Celano needs a speaking crucifix and a kiss on the road. Francis, dying, names a leper and a delay. A reconstruction that lets Layer 2 overrule Layer 1 is not “richer.” It is a different beginning. Scholarly debate: is conversion here “ethical” (Wolf, Thompson’s caution) or “mystical” (the later lives’ kiss and sweetness as miracle)? The Testament’s language is mystical because it is ethical: sweetness of soul and body. Dualism loses. So does a purely sociological reduction that cannot hear “the Lord led me.” The task is not to pick a campus. It is to refuse a Francis who never needed leading and a Francis who never needed a leper. Conservative readers (inside the order) hold that early narrative cores are sound even when miracles are later paint. Critical readers (Thompson) strip hagiographic jobs to recover a reformer. Hermeneutic readers (Early Documents) refuse the strip: perception is part of what Francis historically became. You need all three methods in the room. None of them gets to invent a saying. The Testament’s theology of initiative is repetitive on purpose. “The Lord gave me” structures conversion, churches, brothers, Gospel form, priests, peace greeting. Matura reads this as vocation received, not self-authored. A high-school culture of personal branding will hear that as passivity. Francis’s life is not passive. He walks, kisses (if Celano is right), strips, sails, hides wounds. Received is not the opposite of strenuous. It is the opposite of sovereign. Keep that distinction when you write the Research Prompt: the speaking crucifix is Celano’s job; the leper is Francis’s. Compare Paul on the Damascus road (Acts 9) only to see the difference. Paul gets a namechanging voice and blindness as sign. Francis gets a smell he used to flee and a sweetness he cannot argue himself into. If you prefer Paul’s weather, notice what you are avoiding: the poor body as the site of revelation. Assisi’s minores had already tasted political victory in 1198. Francis’s refusal is therefore not the peasant’s necessity. It is the winner’s son walking away from the win. That is why Pietro cannot decode it as ordinary charity. Charity, in a merchant house, is display that leaves the shop standing. Francis unmakes the shop. Wolf’s suspicion (spiritual capital) and Francis’s verbs (led, showed mercy) have to share the page or you will get a tract. The Research Prompt stays on this chapter because the order of beginnings is the whole method of the booklet. Do not move it to La Verna. The speaking crucifix is the temptation of a better story. The leper is the document. Privilege Layer 1 or admit you are writing a different beginning. That is a historical method, not a piety. Keep the Research Prompt on chapter 1. Testament versus Celano is the method. Keep it. Do not relocate it. Layer 1 vetoes the set piece. The leper remains first. Big Idea Francis’s theology starts in proximity to the socially dead. Divine initiative (“the Lord gave/led”) does not cancel embodiment; it runs through it. If your Francis begins with birds, you have skipped his first sentence. Practice 1. Two-column transcript: left, Testament leper paragraph copied by hand; right, a popular children’s version. Mark every addition. Write 200 words on what the additions are for. 2. Map “outside the walls” in your own institution (school, church, job). Name the bell — the signal that says “approach carefully.” One page, no hero story about yourself. 3. Read one chapter of Thompson on the conversion years. List three places he distrusts Celano. Do not pretend you now “know the real Francis.” 4. For one week, notice when you help from a safe height (money, post, pity) versus when you actually come close. Private log. No social media. Research Prompt Compare Francis’s Testament (Armstrong/Brady) with Celano, Vita Prima 12–14 (San Damiano voice) and 17–25 (leper). Argue, in 750–1000 words, why a historical reconstruction should or should not let the speaking crucifix overrule the Testament’s order of beginnings. Use Thompson as a third voice. Cite pages. This is the one outside-reading task in the booklet. ——— Chapter 2: Coin, Lady, and the Merchant’s Nerve Illustration for Chapter 2 Lady Poverty is not a metaphor you can retire after the poetry unit. Francis hijacks fin’amor — total service to an unattainable lady — and aims it at the condition his class existed to escape. The scandal is class-specific. Pietro’s wealth is not feudal land. It is cloth, credit, routes, coin. Francis does not flee “the world” in general. He flees the new world that made his house. The Later Rule, chapter 6, is the legal face of the romance: “And let the brothers not appropriate anything to themselves, neither house nor place nor anything. And as pilgrims and strangers in this world, serving the Lord in poverty and humility, let them go with confidence to seek alms.” Pilgrim, stranger, confidence. Those nouns assume a God who still keeps a table. They also assume a brotherhood that will be tempted to renovate the inn and file a deed. The Early Rule’s horror of touching money is not generic anti-greed. It is a refusal of the medium of the mercantile revolution. The Later Rule keeps the nerve in writing and then invents the valve. Chapter 4 is the command; the “nevertheless” is the institution: “I strictly command all my brothers not to receive coins or money in any form, either personally or through intermediaries. Nevertheless, the ministers and custodians alone may take special care through their spiritual friends to provide for the needs of the sick and the clothing of the others according to places, seasons and cold climates, as they judge necessary, saving always that, as stated above, they do not receive coins or money.” — Later Rule, ch. 4 Read that twice. The first sentence is absolute. The second sentence keeps the first sentence and routes coin through friends and officers. Spirituals will later call the route a fiction. Conventuals will call it how a hospital gets blankets. Francis is already inside the contradiction while still alive. When later “spiritual friends” hold coin the friars will not touch, the sentence is kept and the nerve is at risk. You can defend the valve as inevitable. You cannot call it identical with the nerve. Chapter 5 then pairs the refusal with work, so poverty does not become a performance of idleness: “Those brothers to whom the Lord has given the grace of working may work faithfully and devotedly so that, while avoiding idleness, the enemy of the soul, they do not extinguish the Spirit of holy prayer and devotion to which all temporal things must contribute. In payment for their work they may receive whatever is necessary for the bodily support of themselves and their brothers, excepting coin or money, and let them do this humbly as is becoming for servants of God and followers of most holy poverty.” — Later Rule, ch. 5 Idleness is named an enemy. Prayer is named the thing work must not kill. Pay is allowed as food and cloth, not as coin. That is a different economy from a résumé and a different economy from a professional beggar with a holy face. Francis pairs poverty with work in his own last will as well: “And I worked with my hands, and I still desire to work; and I firmly wish that all my brothers give themselves to honest work… And when we are not paid for our work, let us have rec…

chapters.text: idleness: “Those brothers to whom the Lord has given the grace of working may work faithfully and devotedly so that, while avoiding idleness, the enemy of the soul, they do not extinguish the Spirit of holy prayer and devotion to which all temporal things must contribute. In payment for their work they may receive whatever is necessary for the bodily support of themselves and their brothers, excepting coin or money, and let them do this humbly as is becoming for servants of God and followers of most holy poverty.” — Later Rule, ch. 5 Idleness is named an enemy. Neither is a craftsman who hoards. The pairing scrapes a modern résumé because modern identity is paid function. Francis wants example and the killing of idleness, not a wage as proof of worth. Pride in patches is already infidelity. Poverty that looks in the mirror has married a different lady. The public nude scene before Bishop Guido is a legal act: clothes returned, paternal authority refused, ecclesiastical covering accepted. Pietro is not a cartoon. He is a merchant watching inventory become masonry for a chapel that will not profit him. Family rupture is the cost, not a side effect. Scholarly debate: Lambert and Burr map the later Spiritual/Conventual war onto this fuse. The Rule of 1223 says the brothers should appropriate nothing and go as pilgrims and strangers. The Testament is hotter: work with hands, no special privileges, lesser brothers. “Not appropriating” can…

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Chapter 3: Few Words, Papal Bull, No Gloss
chapters.text: Illustration for Chapter 3 San Damiano’s voice — “repair my house, which as you see is falling completely into ruin” (Celano) — is the most famous sentence Francis may never have written down. The Testament gives faith in churches and a prayer of adoration instead: “We adore You, Lord Jesus Christ, here and in all Your churches throughout the whole world, and we bless You, because by Your holy cross You have redeemed the world.” And the early prayer: “Most High, glorious God, enlighten the darkness of my heart and give me true faith, certain hope, and perfect charity, sense and knowledge, Lord, so that I may carry out Your holy and true command.” Interior illumination, not masonry, is the petition. The masonry still happened. Literal obedience can be the doorway to a larger repair. Retrospective allegory (chapel = Church) is theologically apt and historically risky if it overwrites Francis’s silence. The form of life, Later Rule ch. 1: “The Rule and life of the Friars Minor is this: to observe the Holy Gospel of Our Lord Jesus Christ, living in obedience, without anything of one’s own, and in chastity.” Innocent III’s 1209 oral approval; Honorius III’s Solet Annuere, 29 November 1223. Between those dates the band becomes an international corporation. Novitiate, examined preachers, permitted study “provided that you do not extinguish the spirit of prayer and devotion” (Letter to Anthony of Padua), spiritual friends, explicit papal obedience. Francis resigns as minister general around 1220. He is a poor administrator who then, dying, tries to bind administrators: “I strictly command all my brothers, cleric and lay, by obedience, not to put any gloss or interpretation on the Rule or on these words, saying: ‘They should be understood in this way.’” He also calls the Testament a remembrance, not another Rule. He wants the bull and the veto on commentary. History rarely honors both. The hermitage rule (Martha/Mary rotation) is the structural critique of specialist holine…

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: Chapter 4: Vestige and the Preposition That
chapters.text: Saves the Canticle Illustration for Chapter 4 The Canticle is not a mood. It is a grammar. Praised be You, my Lord, through… The object of praise is God. Creatures are kin and channels. Brother Sun “bears a likeness of You, Most High One” — likeness, not identity. “Praised be You, my Lord, with all Your creatures, especially Sir Brother Sun, who is the day and through whom You give us light. And he is beautiful and radiant with great splendor; and bears a likeness of You, Most High One.” Bonaventure will systematize vestigia (footprints) versus the imago in Christ. Francis does not write the Itinerarium. He introduces siblings, including weather that is not pretty, water that is “humble,” earth that “governs,” and later pardon-bearers and Sister Death. Lynn White Jr. (1967) blamed Christian anthropocentrism for ecological ruin and offered Francis as exception. The exception thesis can become a way of keeping Christianity as the villain and Francis as an honorary pagan. Sorrell and Delio argue the Canticle is theocentric and Christological. Laudato Si’ (2015) takes the opening as title, praises kinship over mere stewardship, and still refuses to detach the ethic from “the convictions of our faith” (§216) even while noting Francis is “much loved by non-Christians” (§10). Integral ecology’s claim — one crisis, social and environmental — maps onto Francis’s single habit of refusing to treat a creature as object, whether leper or water. That mapping is historically defensible and incomplete. Francis ate meat the Rule allowed. He was not a carbon analyst. His contribution is orientation: gratitude rather than managerial panic. Greccio (1223) is Incarnation staged in hay. Layer-4 wolf stories are parables with a late timestamp. Sort. The Eucharist distinction again: altar is Body; sun is likeness. Collapse those and you get idolatry or magic. Separate them without kinship and you get a warehouse world. Scholarly debate: can the kinship ethic be secularized? The Canticle’s…

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Greeting, the Thousandth Time,
chapters.text: and the Sultan’s Unbaptized Return Illustration for Chapter 5 Peace, in Francis, is not the unattributed poster poem. It is a revealed greeting: “And the Lord revealed to me that I should say the greeting, ‘The Lord give you peace,’ which I previously did not use.” It flattens rank. It echoes John 20. It is ordinary enough to become cheap if you let it. The Canticle’s pardon verse was a civic intervention between podestà and bishop: “Praised be You, my Lord, through those who give pardon for Your love, and bear infirmity and tribulation. Blessed are those who endure in peace, for by You, Most High, shall they be crowned.” Pardon costs. Peace is a crown, not a nap. The Letter to a Minister orders a thousandth reception after a fall. That is not the absence of standards. It is a refusal of exile as the first tool. Damietta, 1219. Fifth Crusade, legate Pelagius, starving city, divided camp. Francis appalled by plunder-as-piety. Early Rule 16: “And the brothers who go among the Saracens… can live among them spiritually… or, when they see it pleases God, announce the word of God.” The or is the ethics. Francis chooses announcement, expects martyrdom or conversion, gets neither. Celano: the sultan listened “with great attention.” Gifts refused. Safe return. No baptism. Later fire-ordeal and secret conversion fail the early-source test (Tolan’s reception history is the map of the projections). Three readings, all partly sourced: missionary, encounter, prophetic protest. A medieval Catholic who thinks Islam false can still refuse a sword and still fail. Afterward he warns against an attack; the army attacks; disaster. That does not make him Clausewitz. It makes him un-usable as a mascot of victory. Al-Kamil’s courtesy is not a transcript we possess. Celano is a canonization writer (Gregory IX, 1228). Hold the gap. Home-front letters (to the Order, to ministers, to rulers) show the same grammar: Eucharist, priests, temporary power, brotherhood not office. If Damietta is bra…

chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: Chapter 6: Final Seal, Sister Death, and the War
chapters.text: Over a Will Illustration for Chapter 6 La Verna, September 1224. Celano’s seraph, nails, side. Companions see. Francis hides. Pain, not branding. First widely attested stigmatic. After him, more. Dante: “from whom Christ took the final seal” (Paradiso XI). Francis’s own near-silence on the wounds, beside loud Eucharistic speech, should control interpretation. He will not make his body the sacrament. The altar already is. Mechanism: miracle, psychosomatic Passion-imitation, chronic disease (malaria, malnutrition, possible tuberculoid lesions). 1224 has no lab. Thompson will not let you be glib. Vauchez tracks sanctity’s transformation: holiness becomes bodily participation, not only wonder-working. Meaning can be Christological while mechanism stays open. Sneering at either inquiry is cheap. Sister Death, last layer of the Canticle, deathbed at the Portiuncula, 3 October 1226: “Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no living man can escape. Woe to those who die in mortal sin. Blessed are those whom death will find in Your most holy will, for the second death shall do them no harm.” Woe and blessing. Not slush. The only surviving autograph is not a wound-report. It is a blessing on a scrap, still in Assisi: “Blessing and all good, the Lord give you. Brother Francis.” — Blessing of Brother Leo (autograph, c. 1224–1225) Master refused in a signature. Esser on the autograph is the scholarly reminder: the one scrap in his hand chooses “Brother.” The Praises of God, written for Leo on the same season’s parchment, is not a tag. It is a list. Humility is a divine name, which is why display would be a different god: “You are holy, Lord God, the only God, who does wonderful things. You are strong. You are great. You are the Most High. You are love. You are wisdom. You are humility. You are patience.” — *Praises of God* (for Brother Leo) If humility is what God is, stigmata as spectacle would contradict the theology of the wounds. Hiding is doctri…

chapters.label: Chapter 9
chapters.title: Chapter 2 gave you the fuse. Chapter 6 gives you the explosion. Do not collapse them. The
chapters.text: founder’s last words were formally overruled: the Testament was judged not a legal document. Charismatic authority lost to institutional authority inside the house he founded. That loss is part of the history, not a later misunderstanding. Hagiography problem (your Layer 1–5): Bonaventure’s Legenda Maior unifies a saint and sidelines messier lives. Fioretti makes a folk hero. Modern Early Documents (Armstrong, Hellmann, Short) try to let the layers argue. The closer to Francis’s voice, the more anxious, sacramental, commanding, un-cute. Conversion, San Damiano, Damietta, and La Verna all change shape as you climb the ladder. Celano writes to support a canonization. Bonaventure writes to unify an order already splitting over poverty. The Fioretti writers write to make a lovable lay saint. Thompson writes to weigh. If you only read Layer 4, you will love him and not know him. If you only read Layer 5, you will know about him and never hear him. Open questions (not closed here): Clare and gender; reluctant authority; crusade compromise; limits of Christocentric “universalism.” Clare’s Privilege of Poverty arrived on her deathbed. Francis supported her spiritually and did not build her the male order’s legal house. He resigned ~1220; the Testament reads anxious. He walked to the sultan with crusade sanction and did not denounce the war as such. He honored al-Kamil without becoming a pluralist. A statue that hides those is a recruitment tool. Thomas of Celano describes black marks and a side that often bled: more restrained than later art. Francis does not write the spectacle. Interpretation is theological: conformity becoming participation; seraph as burning love united to crucifixion. Medical options stay open: psychosomatic Passion-attention, pre-existing disease (malaria, malnutrition, possible tuberculoid lesions)…

chapters.text: agency’s “humility.” A refusal of majores. Assisi taught him the word.

chapters.label: Chapter 11
chapters.title: Chapter 6’s pilgrims and strangers is Exodus language without a map app. Confidence in
chapters.text: alms is either faith or a scam. Francis knows both exist. He still commands confidence. That command will be abused by idle men. He still will not make wages the proof of a calling. Your internship culture will find this either romantic or offensive. Both reactions are data. Spiritual friends, once introduced, become the whole later controversy in seed. If you can already see how a valve becomes a pipeline, you are ready for Burr. If you cannot, you are still treating poverty as a feeling. Damietta without the soundtrack (use with chapter 5) Remove the film score. You have a barefoot deacon, one companion, a year-plus siege, a cultured sultan, a papal legate, gambling soldiers, a Rule that already imagined this walk, a safe return, no baptism, a warning ignored, a later library of fire and secret conversions. Tolan’s service is to show you your century in the story. What does our century need Francis to have been? Dialoguer, because we fear religion. Missionary, because we fear relativism. items.text: Francis of Assisi: The Boy Who Learned a New Family WisdomForge Booklet — Ages 5–10 Francis of Assisi: The Boy Who Learned a New Family WisdomForge Booklet — Ages 5–10 ——— About This Book A long time ago, in a hill town in Italy called Assisi, there lived a boy named Francis. His father sold cloth. His house had good food and fine clothes. Francis liked songs, parties, and shiny armor. He wanted to be a knight. Then something changed. It did not change all at once, like a light turning on. It changed the way a seed grows — slowly, and then all at once you notice it. Francis stopped running from people he used to fear. He stopped clutching things. He started calling the sun his brother and the moon his sister. He walked across a war to talk instead of fight. When he was dying, he even called death a sister. This booklet tells six stories from Francis's life. Each one has a story, words he really said (or words people who knew him wrote down), a big idea, something to try, and a question to ask a grown-up. The questions are not tests. They are doors. Francis loved God. He loved Jesus. He loved people who were sick and people who were poor. He loved birds and water and fire. He did not worship the birds. He praised the God who made them. Keep that straight, and the stories stay true. ——— Chapter 1: The Thing That Tasted Bitter Illustration for Chapter 1 Francis grew up behind stone walls. Assisi sat on a hill. Below the town, outside the walls, lived people nobody wanted to see. They had a terrible sickness. People called them lepers. The town said they must ring a bell so others could step away. Some people treated them as if they were already dead. Francis was not a mean boy. He was a rich boy. He had been taught, without anyone needing to say it in a classroom, that a leper was something to fear. The sight of them, he later said, seemed too bitter. He had already learned other hard things. He went to war with other young men of Assisi against a nearby city. He was captured. He spent a long time as a prisoner. He got sick. His father paid to bring him home. The parties did not taste the same after that. One day the Lord led him among the people he most wanted to avoid. Francis did not write a long adventure story about it. He wrote only a few lines, near the end of his life, when he was trying to tell his brothers what had really started everything. He showed mercy. He did not stay on his horse and throw coins from a safe height. He came close. When he left them, the bitterness had changed. It had become sweetness — in his soul, and in his body too. That is his own word: sweetness. Not a rule he learned. A taste that changed. After that, Francis still lived in his father's house for a while. He still struggled. He visited the sick more often. He gave away more than his father liked. The seed had been planted. The rest of his life grew from that closeness, not from a fancy speech. Notice what Francis does not say. He does not say, "I figured out a clever idea about kindness." He says the Lord led him. He says he showed mercy. He says the feeling in his body changed. Mercy, for him, was not a poster on a wall. It was hands and feet going where they did not want to go. Umbria had leper houses outside the walls the way some towns have a dump — out of sight, out of mind. Law treated a leper as if life were already over: property gone, marriage ended, church doors shut. When Francis came close, he was not only being nice to a sick man. He was saying, without a speech, that this person still belonged to the human family. If you remember only one thing from this chapter, remember this: Francis did not begin by writing a book. He began by going toward a person he had been taught to fear. Words to Remember "When I was in sin, it seemed too bitter a thing to see lepers. And the Lord Himself led me among them and I showed mercy to them. And when I departed from them, what had seemed bitter to me was changed into sweetness of soul and body." > — Francis, *Testament* (1226) Plain English: Francis used to feel sick when he saw people everyone avoided. God led him close. Mercy changed the feeling. Big Idea A hard heart can change when a person moves toward someone they were taught to fear — not by pretending the fear isn't there, but by showing mercy anyway. Try This 1. Draw two faces: "bitter" and "sweet." Under them, write one person or group you are shy of. Do not write a mean name. Write a kind one. 2. With a grown-up, choose one small kindness you can actually do this week for someone who is left out — a hello, a seat saved, a drawing given. 3. Act out getting off an imaginary horse. Practice slowing down instead of rushing past. Ask a Grown-Up Who taught you to be afraid of someone, and who taught you to come close? ——— Chapter 2: The Lady He Served Illustration for Chapter 2 Francis's father, Pietro, sold cloth. Cloth was money you could wear. Fine fabric meant you belonged with the people who mattered in town. Francis had worn those clothes. He had wanted to be a knight, which also meant armor and a horse and a name people cheered. After the leper, Francis started giving things away. He sold cloth that was not only his. His father was furious. This was not a small gift from extra coins. This was the shop walking out the door. Francis had a strange way of talking about what he wanted instead. He did not say, "I would like fewer toys." He spoke as if poverty were a lady — Lady Poverty — the way singers in his time sang about a noble lady they would serve forever. Other young men sang about castles. Francis sang about having nothing to clutch. Why? Because he believed Jesus was poor. Born in a place for animals. No house of his own. Dying with even his clothes taken. If God chose to be poor, Francis thought, then following God meant loosening your hands. Poverty, for Francis, was not a contest to see who could be most miserable. He warned his brothers not to be proud of being poor. Pride in your old coat is still pride. He wanted to be free. If you own a pile of things, you spend your day guarding the pile. If you own nothing, you can look at people. You can look at God. You can work with your hands and, if you must, knock on a door and ask for bread. He also wanted to be a brother, not a boss. People who own a lot often stand on a step above other people. Francis wanted the same step as everyone else — even lower. His brothers were called Friars Minor: lesser brothers. He insisted they work. "I worked with my hands, and I still desire to work," he wrote near the end of his life. If they were not paid, they could ask for bread from door to door — "the Lord's table," he called it — but they were not to become professional idlers with a holy look on their faces. One day, in the square of Assisi, the fight with his father came into the open. Francis took off the clothes that belonged to Pietro and gave them back. He said he now had a Father in heaven. The bishop covered him. It was a hard day for a family. It was the day Francis stopped pretending he could keep both the shop and the new life. Words to Remember "And let the brothers not appropriate anything to themselves, neither house nor place nor anything. And as pilgrims and strangers in this world, serving the Lord in poverty and humility, let them go with confidence to seek alms." > — Francis, Later Rule, chapter 6 Plain English: Don't grab a house and call it yours. Live like a guest. If you must, ask for food. Big Idea Francis called poverty a lady he served because he wanted to be free to love God and people — not because he hated beautiful things, but because he did not want things to own him. Try This 1. Pick one toy or extra shirt. With a grown-up, give it away for real. 2. Make a paper crown labeled "Lady Poverty." Write on it three things you can enjoy without buying them (sunlight, a song, a walk). 3. Work with your hands for twenty minutes: wash cups, sweep, fold. Francis wanted his brothers to work, not to be lazy. Ask a Grown-Up What do we own that owns our time — that we worry about more than we enjoy? ——— Chapter 3: Repair My House Illustration for Chapter 3 Outside Assisi stood a little broken chapel called San Damiano. The roof was tired. The walls needed stones. Francis went there to pray. On the wall was a painted cross. The Christ in that painting does not look crumpled. His eyes are open. He looks alive. Francis later wrote that the Lord gave him such faith in churches that he would pray a simple prayer in every one. The old stories say that while he prayed at San Damiano, he heard words from the cross: go and repair my house, which is falling down. Francis took the words the way a builder would. He carried stones. He begged for help. He even sold things to pay for repairs — which made his father angrier. He also prayed a prayer that we still have, from those early days: "Most High, glorious God, enlighten the darkness of my heart and give me true faith, certain hope, and perfect charity." That is not a nature song. That is a young man asking God to fix the inside of him. Friends began to gather. They did not start as a big organization with offices. They started as a small band who wanted to live the Gospel in a few words. Francis later wrote the sentence that still opens the Rule: "The Rule and life of the Friars Minor is this: to observe the Holy Gospel of Our Lord Jesus Christ, living in obedience, without anything of one's own, and in chastity." Chastity, for them, meant belonging to God with their whole lives, not grabbing people as if people were things. Francis said no one showed him a plan. The Most High showed him to live according to the Holy Gospel. He had it written simply. A pope said yes. In churches he prayed another line he never got tired of: "We adore You, Lord Jesus Christ, here and in all Your churches throughout the whole world, and we bless You, because by Your holy cross You have redeemed the world." They worked with their hands. They preached with short, good words, not long showing-off sermons. They were not to touch money. They were to be lesser brothers, not greater ones. Later the group grew huge. Rules had to get clearer. Francis worried the simple life would be explained away. Near the end of his life he told his brothers not to put a clever twist on the Rule — not to say, "What he really meant was…" He wanted the words kept simple. That fight would go on after he died. You do not need the whole fight yet. You need the first stone in Francis's hand, and the first friends walking with him. San Damiano would later become a home for Clare, a woman of Assisi who wanted the same poor life. Francis did not do this work alone. Words to Remember "Most High, glorious God, enlighten the darkness of my heart and give me true faith, certain hope, and perfect charity, sense and knowledge, Lord, so that I may carry out Your holy and true command." > — Francis, Prayer before the Crucifix at San Damiano Plain English: God, light up the dark in me. Give me real faith, hope, and love, so I can do what you actually want. Big Idea Francis started by fixing a broken chapel. The bigger repair was a Church that had gotten rich and forgetful — and a heart that needed light. Try This 1. With a grown-up, pick one real repair: a torn book, a wobbly chair, a messy corner of a church or classroom. Fix it with your hands. 2. Copy the San Damiano prayer in your own letters. Pray it once slowly. 3. Build a tiny chapel from blocks, then knock one wall down and rebuild it together. Talk about what "repair" means besides buildings. Ask a Grown-Up If someone said "repair my house" to our family, what house would we start with — our rooms, our church, or the way we treat people? ——— Chapter 4: Brother Sun, Sister Water Illustration for Chapter 4 Francis did not think the world was God. He thought the world was God's. That little word 's matters. When he was old, nearly blind, and very sick, he made a song in the la…

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: Chapter 4: Brother Sun, Sister Water
chapters.text: Illustration for Chapter 4 Francis did not think the world was God. He thought the world was God's. That little word 's matters. When he was old, nearly blind, and very sick, he made a song in the language people actually spoke in Umbria — not only church Latin. We call it the Canticle of the Creatures, or the Canticle of Brother Sun. He praised God through the creatures, the way you might thank a cook through the taste of bread. He called the sun Sir Brother Sun — beautiful, radiant, a likeness of the Most High, not the Most High himself. He called the moon and stars sisters. He thanked God through Brother Wind and every kind of weather. Sister Water was useful, humble, precious, and chaste — clean. Brother Fire was playful and strong. Sister Mother Earth feeds us with fruits, flowers, and herbs. "Praised be You, my Lord, through Sister Water, which is very useful and humble and precious and chaste." > "Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Mother Earth, who sustains and governs us, and who produces various fruits with colored flowers and herbs." This is a family song. Families take care of each other. You do not kick your sister. You do not waste your brother. You do not pretend you made the sun. Old stories say Francis preached to birds and picked worms off the road so they would not be stepped on. Some of those stories were written down later and grew like garden vines. The song itself is Francis's own. Start there. The song is enough to teach the idea: everything made is a sibling in God's house, and people are not the only ones who get to praise. In 1223, at a place called Greccio, Francis asked for a live manger scene — real animals, real straw — so people could see that God came into a real world, not a pretend one. Christmas, for him, belonged with hay and breath and cold air. If someone tells you Francis was only an animal saint who forgot Jesus, they have not read the song carefully. The first words are "Most High, all-powerful, good Lord." The cre…

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Lord Give You Peace
chapters.text: Illustration for Chapter 5 Francis taught his brothers a greeting: "The Lord give you peace." He said the Lord showed him to say it. He had not used it before. In his town, greetings could be like little ladders. You spoke one way to a rich man and another way to a servant. Francis's greeting was the same for everyone. It wished them a gift nobody could buy. He also added lines to his Canticle when Assisi's bishop and the city leader were fighting. He sent brothers to sing them in front of both men: "Praised be You, my Lord, through those who give pardon for Your love, and bear infirmity and tribulation. Blessed are those who endure in peace, for by You, Most High, shall they be crowned." The song was not only about weather. It was about making up. Pardon, in that verse, is not cheap. The people who pardon also bear trouble. Peace is a crown, not a nap. Francis wrote to a leader in his order that if a brother fell into sin a thousand times, he should be received back. That is a hard kind of peace. It is not pretending nothing happened. It is refusing to throw a person away. The bravest peace story is from a war. In 1219, during a crusade in Egypt, Christian soldiers were attacking a city called Damietta. Francis did not like what he saw in the camp — men fighting for loot more than for God. He and a brother named Illuminatus crossed toward the Muslim camp. They could have been killed. They were beaten and brought to the Sultan, al-Kamil. We do not have a tape recording of their talk. The earliest writer says the Sultan listened with great attention and was kind. Francis did not make the Sultan a Christian. The Sultan did not make Francis a soldier. Francis refused gifts and was sent back alive. Later tales added fire-walking and secret baptisms. Those later tales are not the solid center. The solid center is: he went, he talked, he came back. chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: Chapter 6: Sister Bodily Death
chapters.text: Illustration for Chapter 6 Francis got sicker and sicker. His eyes hurt. His body was tired from years of hard living. In 1224, on a mountain called La Verna, while he was praying about Jesus on the cross, something happened that his friends never forgot. Marks like nail wounds showed on his hands and feet, and a wound in his side. The brothers who cared for him saw them. Francis tried to hide them with gloves and shoes. He did not show them off. People still argue about how those marks came. This booklet will not pretend we have a doctor's chart from 1224. What we can say without guessing: Francis spent his life trying to be like Jesus, especially Jesus who loved and suffered. At the end, his body carried signs of that love. His friends treated the marks as real. Near death, at a little place called the Portiuncula, he added the last verse to his Canticle. He praised God through Sister Bodily Death, from whom no living person escapes. He warned that dying turned away from God is a true grief. He blessed those whom death finds in God's will. Then he asked his brothers to sing. He had written a tiny blessing for Brother Leo on a scrap of parchment, in his own hand — the only writing we still have in Francis's handwriting: "Blessing and all good, the Lord give you. Brother Francis." He could have signed "master." He signed "brother." He also wrote praises that sound like a list of who God is: "You are love, You are wisdom, You are humility, You are patience." Humility sits in that list as if it belongs to God, not only to shy people. That is how Francis thought: God is not a bully on a cloud. God is the Most High who chose a manger and a cross. Francis died on the night of October 3, 1226. People still tell extra stories that grew later, like fairy-tale vines. Some are lovely. They are not the same as his own words. His own words are enough: mercy that turned bitter to sweet, a Rule in few words, a song to Brother Sun, a greeting of peace, and a last praise through S…

items.text: Francis of Assisi: Gospel Without Gloss WisdomForge Booklet — Ages 11–14 Francis of Assisi: Gospel Without Gloss WisdomForge Booklet — Ages 11–14 ——— About This Book Francis of Assisi (1181/82–1226) is easy to like and easy to get wrong. Posters give you a bird on a finger. Garden statues give you a tame wolf. A modern prayer that begins "Lord, make me an instrument of your peace" gets printed on his name even though he did not write it. The historical Francis is sharper. He was the son of a cloth merchant in a town tearing itself between knights and merchants. He spent a year as a prisoner of war. He kissed the social dead. He stripped in a public square. He asked a pope to approve a life of no property. He walked into a crusader war and talked with a sultan. He died singing. His own last document told his brothers not to "gloss" the Rule — not to explain the hard parts into something easier. This booklet is for readers who can hold a timeline, a tension, and a primary quote at the same time. Six chapters. Same life as the elementary stories, different job: you get the institutions, the arguments, and the difference between Francis's writings and later legend. Read slowly. Francis is not a mascot for whatever you already believe. ——— Chapter 1: When Bitter Became Sweet Illustration for Chapter 1 Assisi in Francis's youth was not a quiet postcard. Twelfth-century Italian towns were going through a communal revolution: merchants wanted a say, nobles wanted their old honor, and the countryside still fed everyone. Pietro di Bernardone dealt in cloth — a business tied to trade routes, credit, and display. Francis grew up knowing how to spend, feast, and dream of knighthhood. He later named that life with one blunt word: sin. In 1202 Assisi fought Perugia. Francis was captured at Collestrada and held for about a year. Prison, illness, and ransom do not automatically make a saint. They can make a person restless. The sources agree he came home changed in mood before he was changed in vocation. The turning point he himself chose to remember was not a battlefield and not a voice from a crucifix. It was lepers. Medieval law and custom treated leprosy as a social death: live outside the walls, announce yourself, stay out of churches, lose ordinary legal standing. The disease was read as a curse you could catch with your eyes. Francis writes in the Testament (1226): "The Lord gave me, Brother Francis, thus to begin doing penance in this way: for when I was in sin, it seemed too bitter a thing to see lepers. And the Lord Himself led me among them and I showed mercy to them. And when I departed from them, what had seemed bitter to me was changed into sweetness of soul and body. And afterwards I delayed a little and left the world." Watch the verbs. The Lord gave and led. Francis showed mercy and departed. The change is bodily — bitter to sweet — not a theory he adopted in a library. Later biographies (Thomas of Celano, 1228; Bonaventure, 1260) add a horse, a kiss, a blessing on the road. Those scenes may preserve memory; they may also polish it. Francis's own version is enough: proximity first. That order matters. A lot of religious people start with an idea and hope their habits catch up. Francis starts with a person his culture had declared untouchable. Kinship with creation, later, grows from kinship with the rejected. If you reverse that order, you get a nature lover who never had to change his social map. He did not "leave the world" the same afternoon. He still lived in his father's orbit. He began visiting the leprosarium, giving away more than Pietro could absorb as charming generosity, and praying in caves and ruined churches. Conversion, here, is a process with a seed you can name. Assisi itself explains why the seed could grow into a public life. The town sat on Mount Subasio's slope, maybe three to five thousand people, on the fault line between papal and imperial power. Upper Assisi held the majores — minor nobles and the Rocca. Lower Assisi held the minores — merchants and artisans. Francis's father belonged to the second group: commercially wealthy, politically hungry. In 1198 the minores drove the nobles toward Perugia and remade the commune. Francis was about seventeen. He grew up watching class war, not a tourist sunset. The money was new money. Cloth moved on roads and credit. Coin, not only land, measured success. When Francis later treats coins as spiritually radioactive, he is not a farmer who never saw a market. He is a merchant's son slamming the door on the very tool that made his house important. Religious unrest filled the same streets. Popular gospel movements — some later condemned, some later approved — were already asking whether the Church's wealth matched the poor Christ. Francis is not a copy of those movements. He is not a Waldensian with a different hat. He stays inside the Church's sacraments and asks a pope for approval. But he breathes the same air: the Gospel, read without professional softening, sounds expensive. Political weather was literal. Imperial troops had sacked Assisi in 1174. In 1198 Conrad of Urslingen ceded the duchy toward Innocent III's orbit. A boy in that town learned that walls change owners. When Francis later greets everyone with the same peace, he is speaking into a place where greetings and loyalties had been weapons. When he fights Perugia, he is not a tourist of violence; he is inside the communal war pattern. Prison in Perugia is not a spiritual metaphor. It is a year of someone else's keys. Leprosy's symbolism did extra cruelty on top of illness. People read spots as God's visible frown. Francis's sweetness is therefore not only compassion for pain. It is a refusal of a purity system. Touch, in that world, was a sentence. Mercy rewrote the sentence without a committee. Kenneth Baxter Wolf and others have asked an uncomfortable question: did Francis need the leper more than the leper needed Francis — a rich boy's spiritual drama using a sick man's body as a stage? The Testament will not let you answer easily. Francis does not congratulate himself. He names bitterness, leading, mercy, sweetness, delay, leaving. There is no victory lap. Still, the question is fair to carry. Charity that needs an audience is not what he describes. Charity that writes itself into a last will might be. Read him generously and suspiciously at once. That is middle-school, not cynicism. | Layer | What it is | How to use it | |-------|------------|---------------| | Francis's writings | Canticle, Testament, Rules, letters, prayers | First. He is the witness. | | Early lives | Celano 1228; Three Companions; Bonaventure 1260 | Next. Close in time, already shaping a saint. | | Later legends | Fioretti (14th c.), popular wolf and bird tales | Devotion, not a documentary. | Big Idea Francis dates his penitential life from mercy toward lepers, not from a branding moment. The Gospel, for him, begins in a body meeting a body the town had thrown away. Try This 1. Timeline card: 1202 war → prison → leper encounter (c. 1204–6) → San Damiano → 1209 oral approval → 1223 Rule → 1224 La Verna → 1226 death. Place one quote on the card that belongs only to Francis, not to a later story. 2. Journal: name a group your school treats as "outside the walls." Write three sentences about what proximity would cost — not a fantasy rescue, a real hallway cost. 3. Compare two tellings of the leper story: Testament vs. a children's picture book. List what the picture book adds. Talk About It 1. Why would Francis, dying, choose the leper — not the war, not the pope — as the beginning? 2. Is "sweetness of soul and body" a feeling, a decision, or both? 3. When does helping from a safe distance become a way of staying unchanged? ——— If the people your town prefers not to see are not your siblings, who is? ——— Chapter 2: Lady Poverty and the Merchant's Son Illustration for Chapter 2 Francis did not invent poverty. Monks had vowed it for centuries. What he did was theatrical, personal, and economically specific. He took the language of courtly love — the troubadour's total service to an unattainable lady — and aimed it at Domina Paupertas, Lady Poverty. The joke is theological. The world calls poverty shameful. Francis courts her as nobility. Three claims sit under the romance: 1. Christ chose poverty. Stable, no place to lay his head, stripped at the cross. If the Incarnation shows God's character, poverty is not an accident of first-century Palestine. 2. Poverty trains trust. A cupboard with no bread makes "daily bread" a real petition. Francis thought ownership manufactures fake security. 3. Poverty enables kinship. "Mine" draws a line. If you own nothing, you can call a leper brother and the sun brother without a property dispute. The Later Rule (1223), chapter 6, puts the practice in law-shaped words: "And let the brothers not appropriate anything to themselves, neither house nor place nor anything. And as pilgrims and strangers in this world, serving the Lord in poverty and humility, let them go with confidence to seek alms." Francis also refused a lazy reading. The Testament says he worked with his hands and wanted all brothers to work — "not from desire to receive wages, but for example and to avoid idleness." Alms were a last table, not a career. Money itself was treated as a trap: the Early Rule links coin to the devil's offer of the kingdoms of the world. That is harsher than "be generous." It is a refusal of the medium of the new mercantile world that had made Pietro rich. The public break with Pietro happened after Francis sold cloth and a horse to fund repairs at San Damiano. Before the bishop of Assisi, Francis returned his clothes and claimed only a Father in heaven. Bishop Guido covered him. The scene is not a cute rebellion. It is a legal and family rupture. Pietro was not a cartoon villain. He was a merchant watching inventory walk into a ruined chapel. Francis warned that poverty can become a new pride. The brother who advertises his patches has already lost the lady. True poverty, he thought, does not look in the mirror. A harder fact for later chapters: the order exploded from a handful of men to thousands. Buildings, books, and study followed. The 1223 Rule allowed "spiritual friends" to handle money the brothers would not touch. Francis accepted a papally approved Rule and then, in 1226, commanded his brothers not to gloss it. That tension is not a footnote. It is the fuse of the poverty controversy that would split Franciscans after his death. Clare of Assisi, who will get her own booklet, pressed the poor life for women with even less patience for loopholes. Remember her name here so Francis does not swallow the whole story. Francis's poverty also had a joy that later writers loved and sometimes over-sweetened. He wanted laetitia — a gladness that refused grim holiness. Brothers who looked miserable as a proof of virtue had already turned poverty into a product. Holy foolishness, in the early stories, is not clowning for a crowd. It is the freedom of a person who cannot be bought. That is why he could sing and why he could scare his father in the same year. Compare three refusals so the idea does not stay foggy: - Aristocratic gift-giving looks generous and keeps rank. Francis's giving wrecked rank. Monastic poverty is real, but it often sits on a monastery's corporate wealth. Francis wanted pilgrims, not a well-endowed barn. - Modern "simple living" can be an aesthetic with expensive tools. Francis forbade the medium of coin itself, which is harsher than a capsule wardrobe. The Letter to the Rulers of the Peoples (c. 1220) shows the political edge. A barefoot man tells princes their power is temporary, they will die, they should honor Christ's Body and care for the poor. That is not "be nice." It is a reminder that Lady Poverty uncrowns more than friars. Read the Rule's poverty chapter as a travel document, not a slogan. Pilgrims do not renovate the i…
